title: Practice Test 2: Claude Certified Architect Foundations
description:
60 unique scenario-based questions with another random selection of 4 out of 6 scenarios. Domain distribution matches official exam guide weightings. Topics include agentic loop implementation, MCP tool design, Claude Code configuration, structured output, and context window management.

As with the real exam, every question begins with a randomly selected scenario to frame it. These scenarios repeat, and that is expected.

Every question has been validated for technical accuracy and topic scope compliance. Detailed explanations with documentation references follow each question.

Prerequisite: Review the official exam guide and complete Anthropic's free certification preparation courses (or have equivalent hands-on experience).

SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.

QUESTION: The team's /pr-summary command instructs Claude to render benchmark numbers as a table, the design rationale as prose, and follow-up tasks as a checklist. Across runs, Claude still often turns the table into bullets and the rationale into a list. What is the most effective fix?
answers: Mark the formatting instructions as "IMPORTANT" and restate them at the end of the command prompt.
Add an example summary to the command file that shows each section rendered in its intended format.
Run the command through "claude -p" with "--json-schema" so every summary is validated against one structure.
Render all three sections as markdown tables so the output format no longer varies between runs.
feedbacks: Emphasis raises the priority of a rule only compared with the other rules around it. It does not change how well Claude understands what the desired output looks like. When Claude already follows the existing instructions unevenly, stronger wording alone is a weaker option than showing the target format.

The format instructions already exist, so the problem is uneven compliance, not missing guidance. A concrete example that matches the real output, with the table, the prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) and the checklist each shown as intended, is the most reliable way to control format and structure when Claude follows written instructions alone unevenly.

Schema-validated JSON is the right tool when a downstream program must parse the result. It is not the right tool when humans read a summary. Forcing the output into JSON would flatten the table and the prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) into string fields. That removes the per-section formatting the team wants instead of enforcing it.

Putting every content type into one uniform format is the anti-pattern this skill warns against. Design rationale is hard to read as a table, and follow-up tasks lose their checklist structure. The output would become consistent, but it would lose the readability that the command exists to provide.
prompt.explanation:
Summary outputs that mix content types are easiest to read when each type has the form that suits it. Comparative numbers belong in a table, reasoning and narrative belong in prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data), and action items or technical findings belong in a structured list. The command in this scenario already asks for this. So the failure is not a missing instruction. Claude follows an existing instruction inconsistently. When detailed written guidance is in place and the output format still changes between runs, the recommended next step is to add a few-shot example that shows the target output. Examples are among the most reliable ways to control format, tone and structure. They work best when they closely match the real use case. For this team, that means a complete sample summary with the table, the prose paragraph and the checklist all in place. Wrapping the sample in XML tags named example helps Claude tell the demonstration apart from the instructions around it.

The tempting alternative is schema enforcement. Claude Code's --json-schema flag and the Messages API structured outputs feature do guarantee a shape, but the shape they guarantee is JSON for a program to read. A pull request summary for humans is not that kind of output. Converting it into JSON would turn the benchmark table and the rationale paragraph into string values, and the team would lose the format differences it cares about. Use schema enforcement when a downstream system parses the result. Use examples and explicit format guidance when the output is a report that people read.

The remaining options fail for familiar reasons. Adding IMPORTANT to an instruction spends some of a limited emphasis budget. It raises one rule above the less emphasized rules, but it does nothing to show what the intended table or prose should look like. Rendering everything as tables replaces one inconsistency with a uniform format that fits only one of the three content types. That is the same flattening the skill is meant to avoid.

See Claude prompting best practices for guidance on examples and output format control, Structured outputs for when JSON schema enforcement is the right tool, and Claude Code CLI usage for the print-mode output flags.

QUESTION: This team ran Claude Code across 900 legacy modules to extract each module's owner, SLA tier, and data classification from inconsistent header comments into a structured service catalog. Reviewers can manually check only about 150 entries. How should the team decide which entries receive human review?
answers: Measure aggregate accuracy on a pilot of 100 modules and auto-accept all entries if the pilot exceeds 97 percent.
Review a uniformly random sample of 150 entries and auto-accept all remaining entries, since random sampling represents the whole catalog fairly.
Strengthen the extraction prompt so Claude resolves contradictory headers itself, then auto-accept every entry the run produces.
Score confidence per extracted field, calibrate thresholds on a labeled sample, and route low-confidence or contradictory entries to reviewers.
feedbacks: An overall accuracy figure can hide very high error rates on one module type or on one field, such as data classification. If one overall number decides whether any review happens, the team can remove human checks that particular groups of entries still needed. This is a common mistake.

A purely random sample is useful for auditing high-confidence output and for catching new error patterns, but it is not a way to route entries to reviewers. It spends most of the review budget on entries that were probably correct. Meanwhile, ambiguous and contradictory extractions stay unreviewed.

Stronger prompt wording cannot create information that is missing or contradictory in the source, so the model would have to guess. Auto-accepting every guess removes the human check in the places where it is most needed.

Confidence scores for each field, calibrated against a labeled validation set, let the team spend limited reviewer time where errors are most likely. These are the fields the model was unsure about, and the modules whose headers contradict each other or the code. This approach puts the 150-entry budget on the most valuable checks. It does not spread the budget evenly, and it does not skip review.
prompt.explanation:
Human review in an extraction pipeline is a problem of allocating limited capacity. When reviewers can check only a sixth of the output, the goal is not to review fairly. The goal is to review where review changes the result. The pattern that does this has the extraction produce a confidence score for each field. The team then uses a labeled validation set to find the thresholds at which model confidence actually matches correctness. Entries with fields below those thresholds go to humans. So do modules whose header comments are ambiguous or contradict one another. The rest are accepted automatically.

Calibration is what makes this different from a raw self-rating. A model can be confident and still wrong, so an arbitrary cutoff such as "below 7 out of 10" has no known link to the error rate. Measuring the scores against labeled examples turns them into something the team can act on: a threshold that can be adjusted to fit the reviewer budget. Anthropic's content moderation guidance uses the same idea with tiered risk levels, where high-risk items are handled automatically and medium-risk items are flagged for human review (Content Moderation). Using Structured Outputs for the extraction keeps the confidence and classification fields well-formed. However, as the documentation notes, matching the schema guarantees the shape, not the truth, so the review routing must be added on top of it (Structured Outputs).

Each of the other approaches spends the budget in the wrong places. A uniform random sample is the right tool for a different job. It periodically audits the high-confidence entries to detect new error patterns that the thresholds do not yet account for. That is why it adds to confidence-based routing instead of replacing it. Strengthening the prompt so that Claude resolves contradictions itself asks the model to invent an answer when the sources really disagree. It then removes the one safeguard that would have caught the invented answer. Making all review decisions depend on one overall accuracy figure is the most dangerous choice. A 97 percent overall figure can exist together with a 40 percent error rate on one module family or one field. Accuracy must be checked for each segment before that segment is automated. This follows the evaluation guidance that success criteria should match the real task distribution, including its edge cases (Develop Tests).

QUESTION: A developer on this team wrote the shared API conventions into "CLAUDE.local.md" at the repository root. Their own sessions follow the conventions, but teammates who pull the repository report that Claude ignores them. What is the correct fix?
answers: Add the conventions to ".claude/settings.json" as a committed project setting applied to every teammate.
Have each teammate paste the conventions into their own user-level "~/.claude/CLAUDE.md" file.
Move the conventions into the committed root CLAUDE.md so every teammate who pulls receives them.
Import "CLAUDE.local.md" from the root CLAUDE.md with an "@" path so the committed file pulls it in.
feedbacks: Project settings are committed and shared, but settings.json holds JSON configuration such as permissions, hooks and environment values. It does not hold ongoing instructions. Written conventions placed there are not loaded as context for Claude, so the teammates would still not receive them.

A user-level CLAUDE.md applies only to that one user and is never shared through version control. Every future edit would have to be copied by hand again. This repeats the original mistake at a different personal scope, instead of putting shared conventions where the whole team receives them.

CLAUDE.local.md is the personal, project-specific memory file. It loads only for the developer who created it and is not shared through version control. Team conventions belong in the project-level CLAUDE.md, which is committed and loads for everyone who clones or pulls the repository.

Imports let a committed CLAUDE.md pull in other files, but the imported file still has to exist on each teammate's machine. CLAUDE.local.md is personal and is not shared through the repository. So the committed import would point at a file the teammates do not have.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code's memory system has separate scopes. They are easy to confuse because the files look alike. User memory at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to one person across every project. Project memory in the repository root CLAUDE.md (or .claude/CLAUDE.md) is committed, so it reaches everyone who clones or pulls the repository. Project-local memory in CLAUDE.local.md is stored next to the project file. It exists so that one person can keep private notes and preferences for one repository without sharing them. All discovered files are combined into context. So a developer with a local file sees the conventions and naturally assumes that everyone else does too.

The symptom in the scenario is that the conventions work for the author and fail for everyone who pulls. This pattern points to a personal-scope file. Scope follows the file's location, not its content: nothing in the conventions themselves makes them shared. Only placing them in a committed project file does that. Moving the text into the root CLAUDE.md fixes the problem for the whole team in one change. It also keeps one source of truth, so future edits reach everyone through normal pulls.

The other approaches fail in ways that teach something. .claude/settings.json is committed and shared, but it is a settings file for permissions, hooks and environment configuration, not for instructions. Written instructions placed there are not loaded as context. Asking teammates to paste the conventions into their own user-level CLAUDE.md repeats the personal-scope mistake. The copies are then certain to become different from each other after later edits. Importing CLAUDE.local.md from the committed file is tempting because @path imports are a real tool for splitting memory into modules. But an import can only expand a file that exists on the reader's machine, and the local file is, by design, not in the repository.

After the conventions are moved, a teammate can confirm that the project file is actually loaded by checking the memory files listed by /context in a new session. See Manage Claude's memory for the file scopes and load order, and Claude Code settings for what belongs in settings files instead of memory.

QUESTION: Test files sit beside the code they test across many subdirectories, and the team wants testing conventions loaded only when a test file is touched. The rule in ".claude/rules/testing.md" sets its "paths" field to "*.test.tsx", but nothing loads when Claude edits "src/components/Button.test.tsx". What should change?
answers: Remove the "paths" frontmatter entirely so the testing conventions load unconditionally in every session.
Add a directory-level CLAUDE.md containing the testing conventions inside each folder that holds tests.
Convert the testing conventions into a skill in ".claude/skills/" that developers invoke before editing tests.
Change the pattern to "**/*.test.tsx" so the rule matches test files in any directory.
feedbacks: Removing the paths field does make the rule load. But it then loads for every file in every session. That defeats the stated goal of conditional loading and uses context on conventions that do not matter for work outside tests. The fix is a broader glob, not giving up on scoping.

A directory-level CLAUDE.md file is tied to one location. Tests placed next to their code in many folders would need the same conventions copied into every folder, and every copy would have to be kept in sync. Path-scoped rules with a glob exist to avoid this when a convention applies to a file type instead of a directory.

Skills are for on-demand, task-specific workflows that someone chooses to invoke. The conventions would be skipped whenever a developer forgets to run the skill. Conventions for a file type that should apply automatically whenever a matching file is edited belong in a path-scoped rule.

The bare pattern *.test.tsx matches only files in the project root, so a test file under src/components never triggers the rule. The recursive glob **/*.test.tsx matches the extension in any directory. This is how path-scoped rules apply conventions by file type in any location, while still loading only for matching files.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code loads a path-specific rule from .claude/rules/ only when Claude actually reads, writes or edits a file that matches one of the globs listed in the rule's paths frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file). This mechanism saves context. Unconditional rules and CLAUDE.md content are added to every session, but a scoped rule costs nothing until Claude works with a matching file. This design lets a team keep large, specialized conventions (test style, Terraform rules, API handler patterns) out of unrelated work, and no one has to remember to load them by hand.

The way glob patterns match decides whether the scoped rule actually loads. A bare pattern such as *.test.tsx matches only in the project root, in the same way that the example *.md in the documentation matches Markdown files in the root. The recursive form **/*.test.tsx matches the extension in any directory, like the **/*.ts example in the documentation. The team's tests are stored next to the source code throughout the directory structure. So the root-only pattern never matches, and nothing warns about it. The rule acts as if it did not exist. Switching to the recursive glob is the fix. The rule can also list several patterns (for example, adding **/*.test.ts and **/*.spec.*), or use brace expansion such as **/*.test.{ts,tsx} to cover related file types in one place.

Each of the other approaches solves the wrong problem. Removing paths makes the rule unconditional. The rule loads, but the team loses the conditional behavior it asked for and pays the context cost in every session. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are tied to one folder. A convention that applies to a file type across many folders would have to be copied again and again. The docs name this case as one that glob-scoped rules handle better. A skill is invoked on demand for a workflow. It would apply only when a developer remembers to call it, not automatically whenever a test file is edited. Note also that even a correctly scoped rule is guidance, not enforcement. If a convention must be impossible to break, a PreToolUse hook is the place to enforce it.

See Manage Claude's memory for rule loading behavior and glob examples, and Skills for when on-demand workflows are the better fit.

QUESTION: A developer used Claude Code to generate a database migration script. It handles typical rows but keeps failing on null values. The developer has described the problem in words twice, and the script still fails. What should the developer provide next?
answers: Restate the null-handling requirement in the prompt with stronger emphasis markers so Claude treats it as the highest priority.
Switch to plan mode so Claude re-reads the entire migration script and proposes an approach before editing it again.
Paste the full production data export into the conversation so Claude can discover every null variant on its own.
Give Claude a few sample rows containing null, empty, and missing values, each paired with the exact migrated output expected.
feedbacks: Stronger wording or all-caps emphasis is not a reliable way to fix an ambiguous requirement. Two written attempts have already failed because the words can be understood in more than one way: what counts as a null, and what each variant should become. The missing piece is the exact expected behavior for the edge cases, and louder wording cannot provide it.

Plan mode is useful when a task is large, affects the architecture, or has several possible approaches that need review before any edits. This problem is a small script with a clear scope. Its expected behavior on edge cases has not been explained clearly, and planning does not provide that missing specification.

Pasting a whole dataset fills the context window with mostly irrelevant rows. Claude would still have to guess the correct output for each problem row. A few targeted examples with expected results are much more efficient and give more useful information than a large amount of raw data.

Pairs of concrete input and expected output show the transformation without ambiguity, where written descriptions have already been understood inconsistently twice. The examples state which null-like variants exist and what the script must produce for each one. They also serve as test cases to verify the fix.
prompt.explanation:
Sometimes a written description of a transformation has been tried more than once and the generated code still handles an edge case wrongly. The cause is almost always ambiguity in the specification, not a lack of effort or emphasis from the model. Natural language can be understood in different ways: what counts as a null (a database NULL, an empty string, a missing key, a literal string "null"), and what each one should become after migration. Two or three concrete examples of input and expected output remove that ambiguity. Each example states which variant appears and what the migrated row must look like. Anthropic's prompting guidance says examples should be diverse. They should cover edge cases explicitly, so that Claude does not learn an unintended pattern from only the normal rows.

These examples have a second use. The same rows and expected outputs become test cases. The recommended Claude Code workflow for tests is to ask for tests of specific behavior, run them and verify the result, instead of only asking Claude to "add tests" or "handle nulls." When you supply examples, it is a useful safeguard to ask for a general solution that works for all valid inputs, not one that hardcodes the sample rows. Then the examples stay a way to verify the fix instead of becoming the whole definition of the fix.

Each of the other approaches addresses a different problem. Plan mode is the right choice when the size of the task, its effect on the architecture, or competing approaches make it useful to design before making changes. A single migration script with a known failing edge case is not that kind of task, and planning does not tell Claude what the correct output is. Stronger wording or all-caps emphasis in the prompt is not a reliable way to fix an ambiguous requirement. It cannot provide the exact expected behavior that is missing. Pasting a whole production export gives Claude a large amount of data instead of a clear answer. It uses context on irrelevant rows and still never tells Claude what the right result for a null row is. When a written description fails to explain a transformation, show the transformation instead of describing it more forcefully.

See Claude Code common workflows and Claude prompting best practices.

QUESTION: A custom discovery subagent finds every call site of a deprecated helper before the main session deletes it. When its search errors out partway through the repository, the subagent reports zero call sites and the deletion proceeds. Which reporting change prevents this?
answers: Have the subagent keep retrying the failed search until it succeeds before returning anything to the main session.
Have the subagent attach a self-rated confidence score describing how complete its empty result is.
Have the main session repeat the full discovery itself whenever the subagent reports zero call sites.
Have the subagent return a distinct error carrying the underlying failure message instead of a zero-match result.
feedbacks: Unlimited retries inside a subagent waste time and tokens. They can also make the workflow stop and wait forever when the failure is not temporary, such as an unreadable directory. A subagent may try a limited local recovery, but it still has to pass on what it could not fix instead of looping forever.

A confidence number that the model gives itself is not a reliable measure of what actually happened during the search. The model can be confident and still wrong. The main session needs the facts about the error. It does not need a subjective estimate added on top of a result that presents a failure as a success.

Running discovery again in the main session brings the long search output back into the context that the subagent was meant to protect. It also does not fix the root problem. When the main session reads the subagent's report, it still cannot tell a real empty result apart from a failed search.

A search that broke and a search that found nothing are different outcomes, and they need different responses. So the subagent must report them differently. When the report includes the underlying failure message, the main session can decide whether to retry, narrow the search or pause the deletion. It no longer treats a failure as proof that no call sites exist.
prompt.explanation:
The failure in this scenario is silent suppression. An error inside the subagent is turned into an empty result that looks like success. The main session then draws the worst possible conclusion (no call sites, so the deletion is safe) from the least trustworthy evidence. The structural fix is to make the subagent's report separate an access failure (the search could not complete) from a valid empty result (the search completed and found nothing). Only the first one should block a destructive edit. The second one is a real finding.

This matters because of how delegation works in the Agent SDK and Claude Code. A subagent runs in its own isolated context. The parent receives only the subagent's final report, not the tool calls in between or their results. If the report does not say that a search failed, the coordinator has no way to know it. At the tool level, Claude's tool-use protocol already makes this distinction. A failed tool execution is returned as a tool_result with is_error set to true and the error text in content. This is what lets the model reason about recovery instead of treating the output as data. The subagent's final report should be just as honest when it returns to the main session. It should include the failure type and the underlying message, so the coordinator can choose to retry, narrow the search, or hold the deletion and flag the missing coverage.

Each of the other approaches misses this. Retrying until success is the infinite-retry anti-pattern. Limited local recovery for temporary failures is reasonable, but an unreadable directory will never succeed on retry, so the subagent must at some point pass on what it could not fix. Having the main session repeat the discovery defeats the purpose of delegating long exploration work, and the main session still cannot interpret an empty list correctly. A self-rated confidence score replaces the factual error details that the coordinator actually needs with a subjective estimate, and models are often confident in the cases where they are wrong.

See Handle tool calls for how tool errors are signaled with is_error, and Subagents in the Agent SDK for how context isolation means only the subagent's final report reaches the parent.

QUESTION: A developer asks Claude Code to generate unit tests for a payment module, and several of the new cases repeat scenarios already covered in the module's existing spec file. What should the developer change in the next request?
answers: Generate the tests, then send a second prompt asking Claude to compare them with the suite and remove overlaps.
Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md stating that generated tests must never repeat scenarios already in the suite.
Reference the tests directory with "@" so that every existing test file is loaded before generation starts.
Reference the module's existing spec file with "@" and ask Claude to add only scenarios it does not already cover.
feedbacks: This uses a full generation pass to produce work that is then thrown away. The comparison step also still needs the existing tests in order to work. Providing the spec file at the start prevents the duplicates instead of cleaning them up afterward.

CLAUDE.md is advisory guidance that loads into every session. A general rule does not tell Claude which scenarios a particular spec file already covers. Without the existing tests in context, the model still has to guess what is covered, so duplicates are still likely.

Referencing a directory with "@" gives a list of file names, not their contents. Claude would learn that spec files exist, but not which cases they contain. To make the coverage visible, the relevant test files themselves need to be referenced.

Referencing the spec file with "@" puts its actual contents in the prompt, so Claude can see which scenarios already exist before it proposes new ones. This combines a concrete file with an explicit instruction to cover only the gaps. It follows the recommended pattern: point Claude at a reference and be specific about the task.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code generates tests from whatever it can see. When it reads existing test files, it matches the project's framework, style and assertion patterns, and it can also tell which behaviors are already tested. The duplicates in this scenario happen because the spec file was never part of the request. Claude knew the module but not its existing coverage, so it tested the obvious paths a second time.

The fix is to give Claude the file directly. An "@" file reference includes the file's content in the prompt (as long as it fits within the Read tool's token limit). Pair it with a clear instruction such as "add tests only for scenarios this file does not already cover". This turns a vague "add tests" request into one based on the real test suite. The official guidance repeats the same prompting principle in many places: point at a reference, name the specific scenario, and state constraints instead of hoping the model will infer them.

The other approaches fail for different reasons. A CLAUDE.md rule is read at the start of every conversation. It is useful for persistent instructions such as the preferred test runner or how to run the suite. But it is advisory and cannot provide the facts about each module that Claude needs. If it tried to hold the suite contents, it would also make every session much larger. Referencing the tests directory with "@" looks like it loads everything, but a directory reference shows a list of files, not their contents, so the coverage is still not visible. A second comparison prompt is a retry that still depends on the spec file being provided. It wastes the first pass instead of preventing the duplication.

See Reference files and directories, Common workflows, Best practices, and Memory.

QUESTION: This team runs a Claude Code coordinator with several subagents to migrate 60 modules to a new logging library. When the process crashes partway through, the restarted coordinator starts over and re-migrates every module. Which design lets the restarted run resume from where the previous one stopped?
answers: Run /compact before each migration phase so the coordinator's context stays small enough to survive a restart.
Add automatic retries so the coordinator re-spawns every subagent after a crash until all modules finish.
Instruct the coordinator to keep a running list of completed modules inside its own conversation context.
Have each subagent record its finished modules in a shared manifest file that the coordinator reads on restart.
feedbacks: Compaction summarizes conversation history to reduce context usage. It is not a way to recover a workflow. Even if a compacted session is resumed later, the summary may have removed the details of which modules were finished. It also has no explicit status for each module that the coordinator can act on.

Retrying the whole workflow is the behavior the team is trying to stop. Every module is migrated again, whether or not it already succeeded. Retries help with temporary failures of a single step. They do not help recover the progress already made.

A session transcript can be saved and resumed, but a list that the model keeps in the conversation is not a reliable record of workflow progress. It depends on the model updating it correctly over many turns. Summarization can shorten it. It also shows only what subagents said in their final messages, not what was actually completed on disk.

When each subagent writes its status and findings to a known location, progress is stored on disk as an explicit record for each module. This record does not depend on any conversation transcript. On restart, the coordinator loads the manifest and sees which modules are completed, in progress or not started. It then sends out only the remaining work.
prompt.explanation:
Crash recovery in a multi-agent workflow depends on where progress is stored. A Claude Code session is conversation history: the prompts, tool calls, tool results and responses of the main conversation. This history is written to disk and can be resumed. But it is not a durable record of workflow progress, and it is not a snapshot of the state of the filesystem. Resuming it gives the coordinator back a conversation. It does not reliably tell the coordinator which modules were fully written to disk before the crash. Subagents make this harder. Each one runs in its own isolated context, and only its final message returns to the parent. A subagent that was still working when the process died never delivered that final message. So the parent's transcript may not contain the progress it made before it stopped, and anything the coordinator was tracking in the conversation may be incomplete or summarized.

The pattern that gives reliable recovery is structured state persistence. Each subagent writes its state (status, findings, which files it changed, any gaps) to a known location. On startup, the coordinator reads a manifest that maps every unit of work to a status such as completed, in progress or not started. The manifest is an application convention built on documented features. It is not a built-in SDK feature, and that is why it is flexible. The coordinator can skip completed modules, send the interrupted one out again and continue with the rest, whether or not a session transcript is resumed. Lifecycle hooks are a good place to write this state. SubagentStop fires when a subagent finishes, and Stop fires before the main agent exits. So state files can be updated at the moments when progress changes.

Each of the other approaches misses this mechanism. Keeping the list in the coordinator's context makes recovery depend on whatever the model happened to write in the conversation. That list may be incomplete, shortened by summarization, or different from what was actually written to disk. Running /compact condenses the conversation, which can remove the per-module detail that recovery needs, and it was never a recovery mechanism. Retrying everything runs the whole migration again, which is the wasted work the team saw. QUESTION: This team's /audit command concatenates four subagents' raw scan output into one long prompt that produces a consolidated report. The report reliably covers the first and last subagents' findings but misses critical issues from the middle two. How should the aggregated input be restructured?
answers: Open the input with a key-findings summary and separate each subagent's detailed results under explicit section headings.
Add a system prompt instruction stating that every section of the input must be weighted equally.
Rotate which subagent's output appears first on each run so that every scanner receives the top position over time.
Run the consolidation prompt a second time and merge both resulting reports to recover any findings that were dropped.
feedbacks: A summary of the most important findings at the very start puts them in the position that the model processes most reliably. Explicit section headings give the model clear boundaries that help it find the detailed results in the middle. This directly counters the position effect in the scenario, and none of the underlying detail is removed.

An instruction to treat all sections equally does not change how attention is actually spread across a long input. The middle content is still processed less well. Stronger wording alone cannot replace restructuring the input so that critical material is in a good position.

Rotation only changes which findings are dropped on a given run. Every time, two subagents' results will still be in the middle, where the model pays less attention. The goal is a report that is complete on every run, not one that is fair on average across runs.

A second run over the same poorly structured input tends to miss the same middle content. Merging two reports adds cost and latency and does not reliably recover the missing findings. Retries address temporary failures, not a systematic position effect caused by how the input is arranged.
prompt.explanation:
In this scenario, findings at the start and end survive while material in the middle is dropped. This symptom is the lost-in-the-middle effect. Models process the beginning and end of a long input more reliably than the middle. In Anthropic's own long-context work, answer passages were placed at the beginning, middle and end of long prompts, and recall changed with position. The content from the two middle subagents is not missing from the prompt. It is in the place where the model is least likely to pay attention to it.

The structural fix is to order the input with position in mind. A short key-findings summary at the top puts the most important conclusions in the first position. Then, even if the model misses some detail later, the report still includes every scanner's critical issues. Each subagent's detailed results should go under explicit, descriptive headings. For inputs with several documents, Anthropic recommends XML structure, such as a documents wrapper with indexed document tags and source subtags. Clear boundaries help the model find and use the sections in the middle of the input. Nothing is removed. The input is organized so that the model's attention pattern helps instead of hurting.

The other approaches do not change the underlying mechanism. Rotating which subagent goes first only changes which findings are missed, so every single report is still incomplete. An instruction to weight all sections equally tries to fix with prompt wording a problem caused by the input layout, and attention does not change because the prompt asks it to. Running the consolidation twice and merging the outputs retries a deterministic position effect. Both runs tend to miss the same middle content, and the cost doubles. Anthropic's context-window guidance makes the broader point. More context, or more passes over the same context, is not automatically better. What matters is choosing and structuring what is in the window.

See Claude prompting best practices for structuring long and multi-document inputs, Context windows for why larger or repeated context does not fix recall problems, and Prompting long context for the background on position effects.

QUESTION: A developer wants a personal, modified version of the team's shared /gen-tests skill for their own sessions. Teammates must not be affected, and the developer still needs to be able to run the team's original /gen-tests on their machine. How should the variant be set up?
answers: Set "skillOverrides" in personal settings so /gen-tests resolves to the modified instructions.
Create the variant under ~/.claude/skills/ using a distinct skill name such as gen-tests-local.
Place the variant at ~/.claude/skills/gen-tests/SKILL.md so it never enters the repository.
Commit the variant to the repository's .claude/skills/ under a separate name so it stays versioned.
feedbacks: The skillOverrides setting only controls a skill's visibility, such as turning it on or off, or limiting how it can be invoked. It does not create a separate skill or replace its instructions with different ones. So it cannot provide a personal variant.

Personal skills in the home directory apply only on that developer's machine, so teammates never see the variant. The variant has a name that is different from the shared skill, in both the directory and any name field in the frontmatter, which is the settings block at the top of the file. So the two skills exist together, and the team's /gen-tests can still be run instead of being shadowed.

Keeping the copy in the home directory does protect teammates, but reusing the shared name causes a name collision. When a personal skill and a project skill have the same name, the personal one takes precedence. Every /gen-tests invocation on that machine would run the modified copy, and the developer could no longer run the team's version.

Anything committed under the repository's skills directory loads for every teammate who pulls the repository. This directly breaks the requirement that teammates are not affected, even though a separate name would avoid shadowing the original.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code loads skills from several places at once. Personal skills under ~/.claude/skills/ apply to every project on that machine. Project skills under .claude/skills/ in the repository apply to sessions in that repository and reach teammates once they are committed. Each skill directory becomes a slash command named after the directory (or after the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) name field). Because these layers are merged, the system needs a rule for when two layers define the same name. That rule is precedence by scope: an enterprise skill wins over a personal one, and a personal skill wins over a project one. This design lets the broader policy layer and the individual's own preferences override what a repository provides. That is useful when a developer intentionally wants their own version of a workflow.

The same rule explains why location alone is not enough in this scenario. A copy placed at ~/.claude/skills/gen-tests/ stays out of the repository, so teammates are safe. But it shadows the shared skill instead of existing next to it. Every explicit /gen-tests invocation on that machine runs the modified copy, and no error or warning appears. The developer can no longer reach the team's original, which is what the scenario says must not happen.

So the pattern for personal customization combines the personal location with a distinct name (for example, a directory named gen-tests-local). Also make sure the frontmatter name field does not bring the collision back by setting it to the shared name. Both skills then load together, the developer chooses between them by name, and nothing changes for anyone else. Reusing the shared name is a valid choice only when you intend to replace the team's version for yourself.

Each of the other approaches fails one of the two requirements. Committing the variant to the repository's skills directory, even under a separate name, sends it to every teammate on their next pull. The skillOverrides setting changes whether and how a skill is visible or can be invoked. It does not replace the instructions with different ones or create a second skill. See Claude Code Skills for the location and precedence rules, and Features overview for how skills work together with CLAUDE.md, hooks and subagents.

QUESTION: The team's /triage command, run with "claude -p" on new bug reports, hands a bug to an engineer when Claude rates its confidence below 6 or the report sounds frustrated. As a result, easy reports written angrily go to an engineer, while hard reports written calmly are left for Claude to fix. Which TWO changes make the hand-off decision reliable? (Select TWO.)
answers: Hand off whenever the fix would require a decision that the repository's conventions do not cover.
Enable extended thinking for the triage step so the self-rated confidence score becomes better calibrated.
Raise the confidence threshold from 6 to 8 so more borderline reports are routed to an engineer.
Replace both signals with explicit hand-off criteria and few-shot examples of fix versus hand-off cases.
feedbacks: A gap in the rules that apply to the change is a real reason to escalate. Without those rules, the agent cannot handle the case correctly, because it would need to make a judgment it has no basis for. When the hand-off depends on this kind of structural ambiguity, the decision follows the real difficulty of the case instead of an indirect signal.

Extended thinking can improve reasoning on a hard problem. But it does not turn a self-reported score into a reliable measure of how complex a case is. The number is still an unverified claim that the model makes about itself. The failure in this scenario is the choice of signal, not the amount of reasoning behind it.

Moving the threshold still depends on a self-rated number. That number is generated text, not a calibrated probability, and the model is often most confident on the hard cases it gets wrong. A higher cutoff sends more easy bugs to engineers without need, and it still does not catch the difficult ones that the rating misses.

Explicit criteria together with examples give Claude a concrete boundary for the decision. The boundary is based on what the bug actually requires, not on how the reporter feels or how confident the model feels about itself. This is the recommended pattern for calibrating when an agent should act on its own and when it should pass the case to a person.
prompt.explanation:
The hand-off decision in this triage workflow is a classification problem over explicit criteria. The criteria are what the bug requires, whether the repository's conventions cover the needed change, and whether Claude can make real progress. Neither of the two signals the team chose measures any of these things. Reporter tone measures emotion. Anthropic's ticket-routing guidance names the emotion over intent failure mode, where a model pays attention to how a customer feels instead of what the customer needs. An angry reporter can be describing a one-line fix, and a calm one can be describing a data corruption bug that spans several modules. A self-rated confidence number is only text that the model was asked to produce. The Messages API returns fields such as content, stop_reason and usage, not a calibrated probability. So the rating has no guarantee of accuracy. In practice, models tend to be confident and wrong on the same hard cases that a hand-off rule exists to catch.

The reliable pattern is to state the hand-off criteria plainly in the command prompt and support them with a few concrete examples. Include a report that should be fixed directly, a report that should be handed off, and the reasoning for each. Examples teach where the decision boundary is, not only the output format. Add a structural trigger as well, such as handing off whenever the fix needs a decision that the repository's conventions do not cover. That trigger connects escalation to a property of the case itself. The same logic applies to other standard triggers, such as an explicit request for a human, or failing to make progress after a limited number of attempts.

Changing the confidence threshold and adding extended thinking both keep the unreliable signal. They only change how it is used. A higher cutoff sends more easy bugs to engineers but does not catch the hard ones that the model judges wrongly. Deeper reasoning does not turn a self-report into a measurement. When an indirect signal does not correlate with the thing you care about, replace the signal instead of adjusting it.

See Ticket Routing for the emotion-over-intent discussion and criteria-based classification, and Working with Messages for the actual shape of an API response.

QUESTION: A developer is replacing ad hoc print statements with structured logging across a large service. Listing every call site would fill the main conversation before design starts. The design and the implementation also need to stay consistent with each other. How should the work be organized?
answers: Instruct Claude in the prompt to report only the relevant call sites and keep every search result brief.
Start a fresh session per phase, recording the discovered call sites in CLAUDE.md for the next session to load.
Delegate the call-site discovery to the Explore subagent, then design and implement in the main conversation.
Keep discovery in the main conversation and run /compact after each batch of search results to reclaim space.
feedbacks: An instruction changes what Claude writes back. But the raw results of each search and file read still arrive in the main conversation before Claude summarizes them. Prompt wording cannot move tool output into a separate context window. Only delegating the search to a subagent does that.

CLAUDE.md is meant for long-term project conventions that every session should see. It is not meant for a temporary list of hundreds of call sites that belong to one task. Splitting the phases across sessions also throws away the shared reasoning between design and implementation, and that shared reasoning is what keeps the changes consistent.

The Explore subagent runs the long search in its own context window and returns only a summary. So the main conversation keeps its space for the phases that must share state. Design and implementation then happen in one conversation, with the full summary of call sites available. This is what keeps the final changes consistent.

Compaction summarizes earlier history to free space. But it runs only after the long output has already filled the window. Repeated summarization can also lose exact details such as file paths and line locations. It treats the symptom instead of keeping the discovery output out of the main conversation from the start.
prompt.explanation:
A subagent is a tool for isolating context, not only a tool for running work in parallel. A subagent runs in its own context window, does its work there and returns a summary to the parent conversation. Any long output that it reads or searches stays in the subagent's context. The built-in Explore subagent is designed for this purpose. It is a fast, read-only agent for file discovery and code search, with Write and Edit denied. It is also intentionally minimal: it starts without the project's CLAUDE.md files and the git status snapshot, so exploration costs little. When Claude needs to understand a codebase without changing it, delegating to Explore keeps the search results out of the main conversation.

This matters for a task with several phases because the phases have different needs. Discovery produces a large amount of output. That output is useful only after it has been reduced to a list of call sites and patterns. Design and implementation, on the other hand, work better when they share one continuous context, so that the agreed approach is applied the same way everywhere. The official guidance describes the same split: isolate high-volume operations in a subagent, but keep work in the main conversation when several phases share significant context. Delegating discovery to Explore and keeping design and implementation together follows both parts of that advice.

Two points are important. A non-fork subagent such as Explore does not see the parent conversation history, so the delegation message must say what to look for. Its report also still arrives in the main context, so asking for a focused summary instead of a raw list is part of the technique. Explore is also one-shot and cannot be resumed. That is fine for a discovery pass, but follow-up questions must go to a new subagent or stay in the main conversation.

Each of the other approaches fails in a different way. Running /compact after each batch only summarizes output that has already filled the window, and summarization can lose exact locations that the implementation phase needs. Asking Claude to keep its search results brief changes only what Claude writes back. The raw tool results from each search still arrive in the main conversation. A brief reply and isolated output are two separate things. Using CLAUDE.md to store temporary discovery results is the wrong use of a file meant for long-term conventions. Splitting the phases across new sessions also throws away the shared reasoning that consistency depends on.

See Claude Code subagents for the Explore subagent and when to delegate, and Context window for how subagents and compaction affect the main conversation.

QUESTION: This team wrote a skill in .claude/skills/ that holds the rule "use named exports, never default exports". Claude follows the rule in some sessions and ignores it in others, depending on whether the skill happened to be loaded. What should the team change?
answers: Move the export rule into the project-level CLAUDE.md so it loads in every session.
Ask every developer to invoke the skill manually at the start of each session.
Add "context: fork" to the skill's frontmatter so the rule survives context compaction.
Rewrite the skill's "description" with more trigger keywords so Claude loads it more often.
feedbacks: A rule that must apply to every session is universal context. CLAUDE.md is the mechanism that loads automatically at the start of each session. Putting the rule there means it no longer depends on whether a skill was invoked, and that dependence is the cause of the inconsistent behavior.

This turns a standard that always applies into an optional routine that is easy to forget. Sessions that skip the step will still miss the rule. It also keeps the mismatch between the type of content and the mechanism used to load it.

The fork option runs a skill in an isolated subagent context to keep long output out of the main conversation. It has nothing to do with whether the skill is loaded at all. The problem in this scenario is loading, not the amount of output or compaction.

The description only makes it more likely that Claude decides the skill is relevant. The skill is still on-demand, and its body is still missing from any session where it is not loaded. A universal convention should not depend on a relevance judgment at all.
prompt.explanation:
The main difference between CLAUDE.md and Skills is how and when their content enters the conversation. CLAUDE.md is memory. Its full content loads automatically at the start of every session. So it is the right place for facts and rules that Claude should always know, such as coding conventions, build commands, and "always do X" or "never do Y" statements. A Skill is on-demand. At session start, only its name and description are loaded. The body of SKILL.md enters the conversation only when a user types /skill-name, or when Claude decides from the description that the skill is relevant to the current task.

This loading model explains the inconsistency in the scenario. A short export convention inside a skill is visible only in sessions where that skill was invoked. Claude seems to follow the rule only some of the time, but in fact the rule was not present most of the time. The project-level CLAUDE.md is checked into the repository and shared by the whole team. Moving the convention there makes it part of every session, and no one has to remember an extra step. The cost is context: CLAUDE.md content is paid for on every request. That is why Anthropic recommends keeping it to short rules that are always relevant, and moving multi-step procedures and reference material that is needed only sometimes into Skills.

The other approaches keep the mismatch. Changing the skill's description can make automatic loading happen more often, but it still treats a universal rule as a conditional one. Asking developers to invoke the skill every session makes the standard optional and easy to forget. The context: fork frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) option solves a completely different problem. It isolates a skill with long output in a subagent, so its exploration output does not fill the main conversation. It has no effect on whether the skill is loaded. Also remember that neither CLAUDE.md nor a Skill enforces anything. Both are instructions that Claude follows. A rule that must never be broken belongs in a PreToolUse hook.

See Manage Claude's memory, Extend Claude with skills, and Extend Claude Code for the full comparison of loading behavior and context cost.

QUESTION: A developer is debugging a legacy billing module across several daily Claude Code sessions while teammates keep committing changes to it. Each new session, Claude repeats earlier discovery work and no longer knows the conclusions reached the day before. Which TWO practices address this? (Select TWO.)
answers: Append each session's findings to the project CLAUDE.md so they load automatically for every developer in every session.
Resume the prior day's session with "--resume" so its accumulated tool results stay available for the next round of debugging.
Begin each new session by directing Claude to read the scratchpad file and recent git history before any further exploration.
Have Claude record confirmed findings in a scratchpad file in the repository as it works, rather than only in the conversation.
feedbacks: CLAUDE.md is for stable conventions that apply to the whole team. Every line in it competes for attention in every request. Filling it with one developer's temporary debugging notes makes it less effective for the whole team. The state of a single investigation belongs in a scratchpad file that is read when it is relevant, not in project guidance that always loads.

Resuming brings back the conversation history. But teammates have been committing changes every day, so the file contents and grep results in that history are out of date and can mislead the investigation. Sessions save the conversation, not the filesystem. When the code has changed, a new session that starts from a scratchpad is more reliable.

A scratchpad only helps if the new session is told to read it. The git log tells Claude what teammates changed since the notes were written. This is the recommended pattern for starting a new context window: first rebuild the current state from the local filesystem, then continue the task.

Findings that exist only in the conversation are not automatically available to a brand-new session. Writing them to a file is what makes them reliably available to later sessions. A scratchpad, such as a progress notes file, turns temporary discoveries into lasting state. Any future session can read it instead of discovering the same things again.
prompt.explanation:
A brand-new Claude Code session does not automatically include the context of earlier sessions. Everything Claude learned during a debugging session is stored in the conversation context: which functions are dead, where a value is changed, which hypothesis was already ruled out. A new session starts without it. Compaction and resume can bring back summarized conversation history. However, the filesystem is the more reliable place to keep task state across a context boundary. That boundary can be a new session, a compaction or a handoff to a subagent. A scratchpad file is the practice of having Claude write its key findings to disk as it works, so the knowledge remains after the context that produced it is gone.

Anthropic's prompting guidance for long-horizon work describes this pattern. Keep structured state, such as test or task status, in a file like tests.json. Keep freeform progress notes in a file like progress.txt. When a new context window starts, tell Claude to review those files and the git log before it does anything else. The two practices only work together. If Claude writes the scratchpad but the next session is not told to read it, the notes go unused. If Claude is told to read a scratchpad that was never kept up to date, it has nothing to read. Reading recent git history together with the notes matters in this scenario because teammates change the module every day. Claude can then compare yesterday's conclusions with today's code instead of trusting the notes without checking them.

Resuming the previous session is tempting because it does restore the conversation. But the Agent SDK and Claude Code session docs state clearly that sessions save conversation history, not filesystem state. When the code has changed since that history was recorded, the old Read and Grep results become out-of-date evidence, and Claude may reason from them as if they were current. When the codebase keeps changing, starting a new session from a short scratchpad and the git log is the more reliable choice. Putting the findings into the project CLAUDE.md fails for a different reason. CLAUDE.md is guidance that always loads, every line competes with every other line for attention, and it is shared with the team. Temporary notes from one investigation make it larger for everyone and weaken the conventions it is meant to hold. Long-term memory features like CLAUDE.md and auto memory hold stable preferences and project facts. A scratchpad holds the working state of one task, and it is read when that task continues.

See Prompting best practices for the multi-window state-tracking pattern, Claude Code memory for what belongs in CLAUDE.md, and Agent SDK sessions for the distinction between persisted conversation and filesystem state.

QUESTION: The automated reviewer judges catch-all exception handlers inconsistently. This team added four examples, each a code snippet labeled only "report" or "skip". Handlers that closely match an example are judged correctly, but new variants still receive inconsistent verdicts. What change most effectively improves generalization?
answers: Have the reviewer assign a confidence score to each handler finding and drop those below a threshold.
Add an instruction telling the reviewer to use its best judgment on handlers that do not match an example.
Expand the example set to twenty or more snippets so more catch-all variants are covered directly.
Add a short rationale to each example explaining why reporting or skipping beat the alternative.
feedbacks: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and it does not change how the model decides whether a handler is a problem. Filtering by confidence hides some inconsistent verdicts instead of making the verdicts consistent. It will also remove real findings together with the noise.

This instruction gives the model nothing concrete to act on. The model is already using its judgment, and that judgment is what is inconsistent. Few-shot examples with reasoning are meant to replace vague guidance of this kind.

Adding many more examples with only labels still teaches pattern matching, not judgment. The model will still fail on any variant that is not in the set. A large block of examples also spreads the model's attention across more text and uses context, and it still does not pass on the underlying decision rule.

Examples with only labels let the model match how the code looks. So it does well on near copies and poorly on variants. A short rationale in each example explains the decision logic itself, for example that one handler hides the error with no record while another logs it and raises it again. The model can apply that logic to handlers it has never seen.
prompt.explanation:
Few-shot examples work by showing a pattern that the model can generalize, and what the model generalizes depends on what the example contains. An example that pairs a snippet with a bare label like report or skip shows the model only what was decided. The model can copy that decision when a new handler looks very similar. That is why the near copies in the scenario are judged correctly. But the model has no information about where the line between the two verdicts is, so any handler that does not match a pattern gets an essentially random verdict. Adding a short rationale to each example changes what the example shows. Now the example shows that a handler was reported because it silently swallows the exception (catches it and does nothing with it) and hides failures, or that it was skipped because it logs and re-raises at a request boundary. That reasoning is the actual decision rule, and the model can apply it to handlers that the examples never mention.

This is the idea behind Anthropic's guidance that examples should be relevant and diverse and should cover edge cases, and that explaining what makes an example ideal reinforces the behavior you want. The examples are not a table to look answers up in. They are a short description of how to judge. Two to four well-chosen cases with a rationale usually work better than a large set of cases with no explanation. The rationale is what lets the model generalize, and the extra examples mostly add tokens and compete for attention. The docs also note that short explanations or evidence are the right way to carry this reasoning. There is no need to ask the model to reproduce step-by-step internal reasoning in a dedicated field.

Each of the other approaches misses the root cause. Adding more snippets with only labels increases pattern matching without teaching the difference between the verdicts, and the next unseen variant fails in the same way. Telling the model to use its best judgment on handlers that do not match repeats the goal but gives the model nothing to judge against. Instructions like "be conservative" have the same weakness. A confidence threshold filters the output of an inconsistent process instead of fixing the process. Self-rated confidence is not well calibrated. In code review, it tends to hide real findings, while the underlying inconsistency stays, and so does the gradual loss of developer trust that it causes.

See Claude prompting best practices and Increase output consistency for guidance on constructing effective examples.

QUESTION: A pull request review from the pipeline returns six findings: three interacting issues inside a shared retry helper and three unrelated single-line fixes elsewhere. How should the developer give these findings to Claude Code? (Select TWO.)
answers: Delegate each of the six findings to its own isolated subagent so the fixes proceed in parallel.
Batch all six findings into one message so Claude resolves the entire review in a single pass.
Address the three unrelated single-line fixes one at a time, verifying each before moving on.
Send the three interacting retry-helper findings together in one message so Claude fixes them jointly.
feedbacks: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context of its own and cannot see what the other subagents are changing. Three subagents editing the same retry helper will produce edits that conflict with or contradict each other. Parallel, isolated subagents suit independent investigations, not problems that share state.

Putting unrelated fixes together with the group of interacting issues produces one large diff. In that diff, it is hard to trace a regression back to its cause. It also spreads attention across problems that have nothing to do with each other. Handling independent issues one after another avoids this.

Independent problems do not limit each other. Handling them one at a time keeps each change small and testable, and if something breaks, it is easy to see which change caused it. This matches the recommended pattern of working in small, verifiable steps with a check after each one.

When problems interact, fixing one changes the constraints on the others. So Claude needs to see all of them at once to produce one consistent fix. If they are given one at a time, the fix for the first finding may be undone or contradicted by the fix for the second.
prompt.explanation:
For a batch of review findings, the deciding question is whether the problems interact. Two findings interact when the right fix for one depends on how the other is fixed. Consider a retry helper with a flawed backoff calculation, a swallowed exception and a missing maximum-attempts guard. These are three interacting findings, because changing the control flow for one changes what the others need. Claude reasons best about this kind of group when it sees every constraint in a single message. It can then design one consistent change, instead of patching the issues one by one and finding the conflict afterwards. The subagents documentation makes the same point about context: when several phases share significant context or need repeated refinement, keep them together in one conversation.

Independent findings need the opposite approach. A typo in a log line, an unused import and a missing null check in an unrelated module do not limit each other. There is no benefit to reasoning about them together, and there is a real cost to mixing them: with one large diff, it is hard to tell which change caused a test failure. Giving them to Claude one at a time, and running the check after each one, follows the common workflows guidance to refactor in small, testable steps. It also follows the best practices advice to give Claude a pass/fail check that it can run and repeat until the check passes.

Each of the two incorrect approaches uses a valid technique in the wrong place. Batching all six findings treats the whole review as one interacting problem, which it is not. The unrelated fixes gain nothing from being reasoned about together with the retry helper. They also lose the benefit of small steps, where each failure is easy to trace. Spreading the six findings across isolated subagents treats the whole review as independent, which it also is not. Each non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context of its own and cannot see the edits of the other subagents. So three subagents changing the same helper will produce conflicting changes. Parallel subagents are the recommended pattern for independent investigations whose paths do not depend on each other. Chaining or shared context is the pattern when later work depends on earlier output.

Group findings by dependency, not by count. For any two findings, ask whether fixing one changes the correct fix for the other. If yes, send them together in one message. If no, handle them one after another with a check in between. When the goal is speed instead of easy tracing of failures, they can also run in parallel.

QUESTION: After Claude Code generates a fix in the pipeline, the team wants a second instance to review that fix with no access to the generator's reasoning. Which TWO practices correctly set up this independent review? (Select TWO.)
answers: Pass the changed file paths and diff explicitly to the reviewer, since it cannot see the generator's prior tool results.
Launch the review as a separate Claude Code run that is given only the diff and the review criteria.
Resume the generation session with a review prompt so the reviewer retains everything the generator already discovered.
Enable extended thinking during generation so Claude deliberates more carefully before finalizing the fix.
feedbacks: An independent instance does not receive the files the generator read, its tool results or its decisions. So anything the reviewer needs must be stated in its prompt. Supplying the file paths, the diff and the criteria explicitly is the documented way to make an isolated reviewer effective instead of uninformed.

A new run has an isolated context window. It contains none of the justifications the generator built up while it produced the fix. Limiting its input to the diff and the criteria is what gives the reviewer a fresh view. That fresh view catches issues that the generator had convinced itself to accept.

A resumed session keeps the full earlier conversation, including the generator's tool calls, results and reasoning. That is the context an independent review must exclude. The model would review its own work while its own justifications are still in view. This repeats the self-review limitation the team is trying to avoid.

More reasoning inside the same instance still has the model judging its own decisions from inside the reasoning that produced them. It may improve the first fix somewhat. But it does not create a second, independent view, so it does not address the root cause.
prompt.explanation:
A second instance works better than self-review because of context isolation. When a model generates code, its context window fills with the reasoning that justified each decision. If it is then asked to review that same code, it tends to confirm those decisions instead of questioning them. A human author does something similar when rereading their own draft: they see what they meant instead of what they wrote. A reviewer that starts from an empty context has not committed to any of those decisions. So it is much more likely to notice an optimization that breaks an edge case, or a cleanup that changes behavior without anyone noticing.

In Claude Code and the Agent SDK, the usual way to get this isolation is a separate invocation or a normal (non-fork) subagent. Each one runs in its own context window, with its own system prompt, tool access and permissions. A fork inherits the parent conversation. A resumed session keeps its full history, including earlier tool calls, results and reasoning. So neither one gives you an independent reviewer. Isolation also has a cost: the reviewer sees nothing that the generator saw. The only content it receives is the prompt you give it. That is why the delegation prompt must include the changed file paths, the diff and the review criteria explicitly. Leaving them out does not make the reviewer more objective. It makes the reviewer uninformed. Anthropic's code-reviewer example in the documentation also limits the reviewer to read-only tools such as Read, Grep and Glob, which prevents it from changing the code it is reviewing.

Enabling extended thinking on the generation step is a tempting alternative because it sounds more careful. But careful reasoning inside the same reasoning context is still self-review. It can make the first draft better. It cannot provide the fresh view that catches what the author found reasons to accept. See Claude Code subagents for context isolation, forks, and resume behavior, and Agent SDK subagents for what a delegation prompt must include.

QUESTION: The pipeline's review findings are emitted through a tool whose "category" field is an enum of "security", "correctness", "performance", and "style". Logs show licensing and accessibility issues being forced into "style", where developers routinely dismiss them. Which schema change best preserves these findings?
answers: Add a self-rated confidence score to each finding so weakly categorized ones can be filtered out.
Add a prompt instruction to report only findings that clearly belong to one of the four categories.
Add an "other" value to the enum alongside a free-text field describing the issue type.
Make the category field nullable so Claude can leave it empty when no listed category fits.
feedbacks: A confidence score does not change the fact that the enum has no valid label for these issues. The model will still choose a wrong category, and it may rate that choice with high confidence. Filtering on self-reported confidence hides the problem later in the pipeline instead of fixing the schema that causes it.

This quietly drops real licensing and accessibility issues instead of reporting them. The team would have missing findings instead of mislabeled ones. It also depends on the model following the prompt, instead of a schema that gives the model a correct place to put the finding.

An explicit catch-all enum value keeps every finding valid against the schema. It also gives the model an honest label for issue types that the list did not plan for. The detail field next to it records what the issue actually is. So licensing and accessibility findings are no longer hidden under style. Later, the team can turn detail values that appear often into full categories of their own.

A null category stops the mislabeling, but it removes the information about what kind of issue was found. Nothing is left to route on or analyze. Nullable fields are the right tool when the data is really missing from the source. They are not the right tool when the data exists but the enum has no value for it.
prompt.explanation:
An enum in a tool's input_schema declares the only valid values for a field. When strict tool use (strict: true) or structured outputs are enabled, that list is enforced as a schema constraint. Even without strict enforcement, Claude is trained to follow tool schemas closely. Either way, when a real finding does not fit any value in the list, the choice that stays closest to the schema is to put it in the wrong category. That is what the logs show. Licensing and accessibility issues end up in style because it is the broadest category available. The schema is doing its job of keeping the output well-formed. The problem is that the label set was designed for the categories the team expected, not the ones the codebase actually produces.

The recommended fix for classification tasks is to put the valid labels in an enum or structured output, and to design that label set with an honest option for findings that fit nowhere else. An explicit catch-all value such as "other", paired with a free-text detail field (for example "category_detail"), keeps every finding inside the schema and records what the finding really is. In JSON Schema terms, the enum is still a closed list. The catch-all only gives that list a valid value for unexpected cases. Over time, detail values that appear again and again show which new categories should become full enum values. This is how a category list can grow without a breaking change. The closely related "unclear" value meets a different need. It lets the model avoid choosing when the source really is ambiguous, instead of guessing. Both patterns follow the same principle: a schema should never force the model to invent a confident answer it cannot support. The tool description should also explain when the detail field is expected, because the schema enforces the shape but the description explains the intent; see Define tools.

Each of the incorrect approaches loses information. A nullable category avoids the wrong label but throws away the finding's type. Nullable fields are useful when data is missing from the source. They are wrong in this scenario, where the data exists and the enum only lacks a value for it. Telling the model to report only findings that fit the four categories hides real issues, and it depends on the model following the prompt instead of on schema design. A self-rated confidence score keeps the forced mislabel and only hides it behind a filter. Self-reported confidence is also poorly calibrated for this purpose. Remember too that your validation code should compare enum values without regard to case, because the capitalization of string enum values is not guaranteed; see Structured outputs, Strict tool use, and the evolving-category guidance in Ticket routing.
