QUESTION: Metrics for the automated review show that documentation and naming findings are wrong roughly half the time, while correctness and security findings are rarely wrong. Developers now merge without reading any findings. What should the team do first?
answers: Tighten reporting thresholds across all categories equally so the blended false-positive rate falls to an acceptable level.
Keep every category active but attach the model's self-rated confidence to each finding so developers can triage faster.
Add an instruction telling the model to apply much stricter judgment to documentation and naming findings before reporting them.
Remove the documentation and naming categories from the review prompt for now, and reinstate them once their criteria are reworked.
feedbacks: Tightening every category by the same amount removes real correctness and security findings. Those are the categories that are already accurate and the most valuable. The problem is limited to two categories. A change that applies to every category fixes the wrong thing and weakens the part of the system that works.

Confidence labels can be useful when a later verification or filtering stage ranks findings by them. But adding them alone does not stop the noisy categories from being reported. Developers have already stopped reading findings completely. Adding another field to each finding does nothing to stop the categories that are destroying trust in the whole review.

A request for stricter judgment gives the model nothing concrete to act on. The model has no clear rule for what to report or skip, so the results stay inconsistent. The noisy categories also stay active while the team works on a fix, so developers keep losing trust in the meantime.

Noisy categories affect trust in the whole review. Once developers learn that half of what they see is wrong, they stop reading everything, including the accurate correctness and security findings. Removing the two low-precision categories right away stops this loss of trust and keeps the trustworthy output visible. It also gives the team time to rebuild explicit criteria and examples for those categories, and to test them on a labeled sample before turning them back on.
prompt.explanation:
An automated reviewer is only useful if developers actually read what it produces. So developer trust is the most important thing the system has to protect. Trust is not lost one category at a time. When documentation and naming findings are wrong about half the time, developers do not learn to skip only those two categories. They learn that the reviewer is unreliable and start ignoring everything, including correctness and security findings that are almost always right. This is the failure in the scenario: developers merge without reading any findings at all.

So the right first step is to temporarily disable the categories with many false positives and keep the high-precision ones running. This is a decision about what to fix first, not a permanent design. The categories come back after their prompts are reworked. The reworked prompts need explicit, checkable criteria for what to report and what to skip, and a few contrasting examples of acceptable patterns and truly problematic ones. The team also needs a labeled sample to measure precision before turning the categories back on. Anthropic's evaluation guidance stresses setting specific, measurable success criteria and testing prompts against cases that match real-world distributions. That is how you know a reworked category is ready to return; see Create strong empirical evaluations.

The other approaches fail for different reasons. Attaching self-rated confidence to each finding keeps the same amount of noise in front of developers. Confidence labels are useful when a later verification or filtering stage ranks or filters findings by them. On their own, they only add a note to the problem instead of limiting it. Telling the model to be stricter about two categories is a vague request for caution with no decision rule. The output stays inconsistent, and developers keep losing trust. Tightening thresholds by the same amount for every category throws away accurate correctness and security findings to make up for two bad categories. That weakens the part of the reviewer that works. Precision problems are local to a category, but the damage to trust affects the whole reviewer. So limit the damage first, and then fix the categories.

QUESTION: The test-generation step in this pipeline emits each suggested test through a tool whose schema marks "existing_test_file" as required. For modules that have no tests yet, Claude fills the field with plausible-looking paths that do not exist, and the pipeline fails when it opens them. What change most directly addresses this?
answers: Add a validation-retry loop that returns the missing-path error so Claude can correct the value.
Make "existing_test_file" optional and nullable so Claude can return null when no test file exists.
Add an instruction to the prompt stating that file paths must never be invented under any circumstances.
Add few-shot examples showing correctly populated paths for modules that already have test files.
feedbacks: Retrying with error feedback works for format and structure mistakes that the model can fix by reading the source again. In this scenario, the information does not exist. Every retry still faces a required field with nothing true to put in it, so the model will invent another path.

A required field tells the model that it must supply a value on every call, even when the source has none. That is the situation where invented values appear. Allowing the field to be missing or null gives Claude an honest way to report that no test file exists. The pipeline can then take a different path on null instead of opening an invented path.

The instruction conflicts with the schema, which still declares the field as required and expects a string value. When a prompt rule conflicts with a schema contract, the result is probabilistic at best. The model still has no approved way to report that the file is missing. So prompt wording alone does not remove the pressure to invent a value.

Examples of correct paths make the formatting more consistent for the cases that already work. But they show nothing about the case that fails. The model still has no permitted way to say that the file is missing, so examples do not change the outcome for modules without tests.
prompt.explanation:
Schema-enforced output guarantees the shape of the data, not its truth. When a tool's input_schema lists a property under required, the model treats it as a contract it must satisfy on every call. When strict tool use or structured outputs are enabled, the presence of required fields is fully guaranteed. If the real fact is missing from the source, the easiest way to satisfy the contract is to make something up, and the result looks just like a real answer. That is why Anthropic's guidance on schema design is to mark a property as required only when it is truly always present. Otherwise, make it optional or allow null (for example "type": ["string", "null"]). Then the model has a valid way to say "no data", and downstream code can take a different path when that happens.

Treat the schema as the contract for what the model is allowed to say about the document, not only what you would like it to say. A nullable field also has a small cost. When strict tool use or structured outputs are enabled, optional parameters count toward a documented complexity limit, and required properties are output before optional ones. So teams should make fields optional only where it is needed, not everywhere. In this case the field really is conditional, so making it optional is the right choice.

The other approaches misunderstand the failure. A validation-retry loop is the right tool for format, structure and arithmetic errors, because the model can check the source again and fix them. It does not work when the required information does not exist, which is the situation in this scenario. A stronger prompt instruction conflicts with the schema's declared contract instead of changing it, so the model is still asked to supply a string it does not have. Few-shot examples of correctly filled paths improve consistency for modules that already have tests. But they never show the model how to handle the missing case. Even if they did, the schema gives the model no approved way to give that answer.

See Structured outputs for required versus optional field behavior and schema limitations, and Define tools for how required and optional parameters are declared in a tool's input schema.

QUESTION: This team's review prompt tells Claude to report only findings it is at least 90% sure about, yet developers still receive comments on naming, import order, and local helper patterns the team accepts. What prompt change best removes this noise?
answers: Have Claude attach a self-rated confidence score to each finding and drop low scores during post-processing.
Replace the threshold with explicit lists of what to report, such as logic and security bugs, and what to skip.
Run the review three times on each pull request and keep only findings that appear in every run.
Raise the stated threshold to 99% and add that only findings certain to be real defects should appear.
feedbacks: Self-reported confidence from a language model is poorly calibrated. A small style comment that the model believes is correct will get a high score and pass the filter. This option moves the same confidence-based filtering out of the prompt and into code, but it still does not tell the reviewer what should be reported.

A numeric confidence threshold gives the model nothing concrete to check, because the model has no calibrated internal probability to compare against. So style comments keep appearing with full confidence. Naming what to report (logic errors, security issues, broken edge cases) and what to skip (naming, formatting, accepted local patterns) turns the instruction into a decision rule that the model can apply consistently. That is what actually reduces the unwanted findings.

Requiring agreement across runs reduces random differences between runs. But a reviewer that always believes import order should be reported will report it in every run. This triples the cost and does not change the underlying judgment about which categories matter.

This makes an instruction stronger even though it already failed at 90%, and it still never tells the model which issue types count as defects. The model was already highly confident about the naming and import-order comments when it produced them. So a stricter number does not change what gets flagged.
prompt.explanation:
The main problem in this scenario is that confidence wording gives the model nothing concrete to apply. An instruction like "only report findings you are 90% sure about" asks the model to compare its output with a probability that it does not actually compute in a calibrated way. The model sees the naming and import-order issues as real, is fully confident in them and reports them. From the model's point of view, the threshold is met, so the instruction never has any effect. Raising the number, asking for self-rated scores, or voting across several runs all leave this judgment unchanged. None of them tells the reviewer what kind of thing a reportable issue is.

What works instead is to replace the confidence rule with explicit categories to report and to skip. A review prompt can say to report logic errors, security vulnerabilities and broken edge cases, and to skip naming, formatting and local helper conventions. This gives the model a classification task that it can perform consistently: every possible finding either fits a reportable category or it does not. Anthropic's own Code Review works this way by default. It focuses on bugs that would break production, not on formatting preferences. The same pattern appears in the REVIEW.md guidance at Customize Code Review. That guidance keeps the Important severity for findings that break behavior or leak data, treats style and naming as Nit at most, limits the number of nits, and lists things to skip completely, such as formatting that a linter already enforces, generated files and lockfiles.

This matters for more than neatness. It matters for developer trust. Each time a developer dismisses a comment about an accepted pattern, they learn to dismiss the next comment too, including a security finding that is correct. So making an automated reviewer precise means defining, in concrete terms, which categories are reportable and which are not. That definition must be in the prompt, where the model can apply it. A confidence number or a post-processing filter cannot recover a distinction that the model was never given.

QUESTION: The review job runs with "--output-format json" and "--json-schema", and every finding parses without errors. However, "ticket_id" arrives as "PROJ-482", "proj 482", or "#482", depending on how the PR description wrote it. The step that builds the issue tracker link then fails. What change best fixes this?
answers: Instruct Claude to copy the ticket reference exactly as it appears in the PR description or commit message.
Add a post-processing step that strips every non-digit character from the ticket string before building the link.
State a standard ticket format in the prompt with rules for converting each variant found in PR text.
Enable strict schema enforcement so the API rejects any ticket value that is not in the standard form.
feedbacks: Copying the text without changes is what already happens, and it is the cause of the inconsistency. The later linking step needs one standard form. It does not need an exact copy of whatever the author typed.

Removing every non-digit character also removes the project key. The link step is left with only a number like 482, and the tracker cannot match that to a specific issue. This destroys information that the standard form needs, instead of converting the value into that form.

The schema already guarantees well-formed JSON. The remaining problem is about meaning: the value is copied in whatever form the source used. Explicit normalization rules, added next to the schema, tell Claude how to convert each variant into the standard form. This is the recommended way to handle inconsistent formatting in the source.

Strict schema enforcement controls structure, types and whether a value is in an enum. It does not understand what a correctly formatted ticket identifier is, and it does not reject output because of its meaning. A string field accepts all three variants equally.
prompt.explanation:
This question is a common example of the difference between syntactic correctness (the form of the output) and semantic correctness (its meaning) in structured output. Passing a JSON schema through --json-schema (or, in the API, through output_config.format or a strict tool definition) guarantees several things. The output is well-formed, required fields are present, and types and supported structural constraints are followed. There are documented exceptions. For example, the capitalization of string enum and const values is not guaranteed. But the schema says nothing about whether a free-text string has the meaning that your downstream system expects. A ticket identifier written three different ways is valid in all three forms as far as the schema is concerned. So the schema cannot be the fix.

The schema sets the shape of the output, and the prompt defines the meaning of the values. When source documents are formatted inconsistently (in this scenario, PR descriptions and commit messages), the prompt should include explicit normalization rules. Name the standard form (for example, an uppercase project key, a hyphen and the number). Then say how each known variant converts to it, including bare numbers that need the project prefix. Claude applies these rules when it generates the output. So the value written to ticket_id is already in the form the issue tracker expects. Anthropic's prompting guidance makes the same general point: be specific about output constraints and formatting instead of assuming the model will infer them. The same technique works for dates (always ISO 8601), currency (a numeric amount plus a code) and units. It is cheap to add because it changes only the prompt text, not the schema. That also avoids the grammar recompilation that a schema change would cause.

Removing non-digit characters in post-processing looks like normalization, but it throws away the project key. Every ticket becomes a bare number that the tracker cannot match to an issue. The pipeline would fail as reliably as before, only for a different reason. Telling Claude to copy the reference without changes only turns the current behavior into a rule. Enabling strict enforcement is a misunderstanding of what strict mode provides. It guarantees that the output matches the schema, within documented limits. The structured outputs documentation states clearly that even enum capitalization is not guaranteed, and the meaning of an arbitrary string is certainly not guaranteed. Strict schemas and normalization rules work together. One does not replace the other, and a reliable extraction pipeline uses both.

See Structured outputs for what schema enforcement does and does not guarantee, and Claude prompting best practices for guidance on explicit formatting instructions.

QUESTION: This team's pipeline writes a test suite before implementation and asks Claude to make it pass. When tests fail, the pipeline re-prompts with "Some tests failed, try again," and runs rarely converge. What change would most improve the loop?
answers: Include the failing test names and assertion output in each retry prompt so Claude can target the actual failures.
Raise the maximum number of retry attempts per run so Claude has more chances to converge on a passing implementation.
Ask Claude to rate its confidence that the implementation is correct before each resubmission and retry only when it is low.
Rewrite each retry prompt with a more detailed prose description of the behavior the tests already expect.
feedbacks: Test-driven iteration works because the failing output tells Claude which expectation was broken and how. Sending the concrete failure back gives Claude the same information a developer uses in a run, read, edit, re-run loop. That is what allows the loop to converge on a passing implementation.

More attempts with the same uninformative prompt only repeat the guessing at a higher cost. Without the failure output, each retry has no more information than the last one, so the rate of success does not improve.

Self-rated confidence is unreliable. A model can be confident and wrong about code that has not been tested. The pipeline already has an objective signal in the test results. That signal, not a confidence score, should decide the next iteration.

The tests already describe the expected behavior in full detail. Restating it in prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) adds words but does not tell Claude which case is broken. Prose descriptions are also understood inconsistently, and concrete tests were introduced to solve that problem.
prompt.explanation:
Test-driven iteration with Claude Code is a feedback loop, and the quality of the loop depends completely on the quality of the feedback. Claude Code's recommended approach to failing tests is to run the suite, read the error output, find the relevant source code, edit it and run the suite again. The error output is the step that carries information. The other steps are mechanical. When a pipeline replaces that output with "some tests failed, try again", it removes the only signal that shows how one failure differs from another. Claude then has to guess which of many possible defects to fix.

A test suite written before the implementation is a specification with a built-in checker. Each failing assertion names one specific expectation that was broken, and it often shows the actual and expected values next to each other. Passing those test names and messages into the retry prompt lets Claude reason about the specific gap, instead of working out the intent again from the beginning. This is also why the best-practices guidance stresses giving Claude a runnable verification check and asking for evidence such as test output. The check is only useful if its results reach the model.

Each of the other approaches misses this. Adding prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) descriptions repeats what the tests already state more clearly and completely, and prose is the form of description that leads to inconsistent interpretations. Raising the retry limit multiplies the cost without adding information, because every attempt starts from the same prompt that contains no failure details. Self-rated confidence replaces the objective signal that the pipeline already has with a subjective judgment. The model has no reliable way to know whether untested code is correct, but the test runner does.

In CI, this means the retry stage should capture the runner's stdout or a structured failure report and pass it into the next claude -p invocation. Another option is to let Claude run the suite itself, so the output appears in its own context. See How Claude Code works for the run, read, edit, re-run loop and Best practices for giving Claude verifiable checks and requiring evidence of success.

QUESTION: The pipeline defines three extraction tools (one each for code diffs, CI failure logs, and dependency manifest changes) and sets "tool_choice" to the "any" type because artifacts arrive unlabeled. Every artifact now returns a tool call, but roughly one in five failure logs is routed to the diff tool. What change best fixes the misrouting?
answers: Rewrite each tool description to spell out what its artifact type looks like and when to prefer it over the other two.
Add a retry step that resubmits any artifact whose extracted output fails validation against the chosen tool's schema.
Change tool selection to force the diff-extraction tool so every artifact is processed with a single consistent schema.
Return tool selection to its default so Claude can answer in text when it is unsure which extraction tool applies.
feedbacks: Setting tool selection to the "any" type only guarantees that some tool is called. Which tool Claude picks depends on the tool descriptions. Descriptions that clearly separate a failure log from a diff, and that state when to use each tool, are the recommended way to improve selection among tools that overlap.

A failure log sent to the wrong tool still produces input that is syntactically valid for the diff tool's schema. So schema validation passes, and the retry is never triggered. Retries address format and structure errors, not the earlier decision about which tool to call.

Forcing one named tool removes Claude's ability to choose a schema at all. Every failure log and manifest change would be forced into the diff schema. That turns an occasional routing error into a certain error for two of the three artifact types.

The default "auto" setting lets Claude reply with plain text instead of calling a tool. This brings back unstructured responses that the downstream parser cannot handle. It also does nothing to help Claude tell the artifact types apart when it does call a tool.
prompt.explanation:
It helps to separate what tool_choice controls from what it does not control. The "any" setting controls whether a tool is called. Claude must use one of the provided tools and cannot give a plain text answer instead. By design, it does not control which tool is called. That decision is left to the model, and the model makes it by reading the tool definitions. In the scenario, the first guarantee already works (every artifact produces a tool call). So the remaining problem is only in the selection step.

Tool descriptions are the main way the model selects a tool. When three extraction tools have short or overlapping descriptions, a CI failure log that contains some code snippets can look enough like a diff that Claude picks the wrong schema. Rewrite each description to say what the artifact looks like. For example, a log starts with a runner header and ends with an exit status, while a diff is made of file headers and hunks. Also say what the tool returns and when to use it instead of the other two tools. This gives the model concrete criteria for the decision. It is the same principle as explicit review criteria in the rest of the pipeline: the model follows clear, concrete distinctions much more reliably than implied ones.

Each of the other approaches misses the mechanism. Forcing one named tool with {"type": "tool", "name": ...} is appropriate when a specific extraction must run first, such as metadata before enrichment. But with mixed artifact types, it ties every document to one schema. Going back to "auto" allows free-text responses again, because the model may then decide not to call a tool at all. A retry based on validation is useful for format and structure errors. But a log sent to the wrong tool produces input that matches the diff tool's schema, so validation passes and nothing is retried. Note that strict: true has the same limit. It makes tool inputs match the schema and makes sure the tool name is valid, but it does not judge whether the tool chosen was the right one for the content.

Forced tool use also has limits that depend on the model. The documentation lists models that return an error for "any" and for forcing a named tool, and it recommends "auto" with strict tool use or structured outputs for those models. So confirm support for the model that the pipeline uses. See Define tools for the tool_choice options and description guidance, and Strict tool use for what schema enforcement does and does not guarantee.

QUESTION: This team wants every automated review finding to carry a confidence value so a separate verification stage can route findings for a second look. Which TWO practices make that confidence useful for routing? (Select TWO.)
answers: Check the reported confidence against a labeled set of findings before using it to set routing thresholds.
Instruct the review prompt to withhold any finding whose confidence falls below a fixed threshold before output.
Run the review three times and average each finding's confidence so routing uses a smoother signal.
Ask the review to report every finding, including uncertain ones, and filter by confidence in a later pass.
feedbacks: A confidence value is a field in the output schema that the model fills in. It is not a probability that the API computes. So it is only useful for routing once you know how it relates to actual accuracy. Calibrating it against findings that developers have already labeled true or false shows which thresholds actually separate reliable findings from doubtful ones.

This moves filtering back into the finding step, which is the job the verification stage was supposed to take over. Guidance for current models warns that cautious or threshold-based instructions in the review prompt make the model report less. The withheld findings are then not available for any later verification or analysis.

Averaging self-reported confidence across runs reduces random differences between runs. But it does nothing to show whether the values match real accuracy, so a model that is always overconfident stays overconfident. It also triples the review cost, and the routing thresholds are still not based on any observed results.

Separating coverage from filtering is the recommended pattern. The finding step reports everything, with confidence and severity attached, and a later verification stage decides what to show to developers. If the review prompt asks the model to filter first, the model tends to report less. Then uncertain but real issues never reach the verification stage at all.
prompt.explanation:
A self-reported confidence field is a routing signal. It only works as one when two conditions are met. First, the finding step must produce the full set of findings, so the signal has something to act on. Second, the signal must be checked against real results before any thresholds are set on it.

The first condition is why Anthropic's code review guidance recommends separating coverage from filtering. When the review prompt tells the model to be cautious or to report only high-confidence findings, the model reports less. The uncertain cases are dropped without any notice instead of being labeled. If the prompt instead asks for every issue, each with a confidence level and an estimated severity, a later verification stage can decide three things: what developers see right away, what gets a second independent check, and what is logged for later analysis. That stage can also do real verification work, such as asking a new instance to confirm a finding against the code, instead of relying on the number alone. See Prompting Claude Opus 4.8.

The second condition follows from what confidence actually is. In a structured output or tool schema, confidence is just another field that the model fills in. Structured outputs are designed to return valid JSON that matches the schema on a normal successful completion. But that is only a constraint on format and shape. It does not make the value a calibrated probability. The documented exceptions (a refusal, or output cut off by max_tokens) can still produce a response that does not match the schema, and code must handle that case. A model can be overconfident on every finding in one category and underconfident in another. Checking the reported values against a labeled set of findings (ones that developers have already marked as real or dismissed) shows where the thresholds should be. It also shows which categories need prompt work before their confidence can be trusted. See Structured outputs.

The incorrect options fail on these two points. Putting a threshold into the review prompt brings back filtering in the finding step, and the verification stage no longer receives the findings it needs. Averaging confidence across repeated runs reduces variance but not bias. Three overconfident scores average to an overconfident score. The routing thresholds are still not based on any observed accuracy, and the review costs three times as much.

QUESTION: A trial ran the nightly test-generation job through the Message Batches API, and every batch finished in well under an hour. A developer now proposes routing the pre-merge review check, which must finish before a pull request can merge, through batches as well to save cost. How should the team respond?
answers: Move the pre-merge check to batches but poll the batch status and fall back to a synchronous call after one hour.
Keep the pre-merge check on the synchronous Messages API and leave only the nightly job on batches.
Move the pre-merge check to batches with "stream" set to true so results are delivered as soon as each request completes.
Move the pre-merge check to batches and submit each pull request as its own single-request batch so it is processed faster.
feedbacks: Developers would still wait up to an hour on every pull request before the fallback runs. When the fallback does run, the team pays for both the batch attempt and the synchronous call. A check that blocks merging should run synchronously, instead of adding a timeout workaround on top of an asynchronous service.

The pre-merge check blocks developers from merging, so the workflow cannot continue until it gets a response. The Message Batches API gives no guarantee about when it will finish, and a batch can take up to 24 hours. So fast trial results do not make it suitable for a required check that blocks merging. The nightly job is still a good fit for batches.

Streaming is not supported inside a batch, because batch results are returned together as one results file after processing ends. Streaming is a way to reduce latency for synchronous Messages API calls. It does not make batch processing respond in real time.

Batch size does not change what the service guarantees. A batch starts processing right away, but it may still take up to 24 hours, no matter how many requests it contains. A single-request batch is still an asynchronous job with no latency SLA, so it cannot serve as a required check before merging.
prompt.explanation:
The choice between the synchronous Messages API and the Message Batches API depends on one question: does anything wait for the result? A pre-merge review check is a blocking workflow. The developer cannot merge until it finishes, so the check needs an interactive response within a limited time. The Batches API is designed for the opposite case: large volumes of independent requests where immediate responses are not required. In return for giving up immediate responses, you get a 50% cost reduction. Anthropic's documentation says that a batch starts processing right away but can take up to 24 hours. Results become available only when every request has completed or the 24-hour window ends. Most batches do finish in under an hour, but that is an observation, not a guarantee. That is why a few fast trial runs should not change the design of a required check before merging.

The nightly test-generation job is a very good fit for batches. Nobody is waiting for it, it runs on a predictable schedule, and a result that arrives any time before the morning is just as useful. Keep that job on batches and keep the pre-merge check on synchronous calls. Each workload then gets the latency guarantee that it actually needs.

The workarounds in the other options all try to force an asynchronous service to act like a synchronous one. Polling with a one-hour fallback still makes every pull request wait, and it can double the cost of the slow cases. Reducing a batch to one request does not change the service's completion limit. Each request is processed independently, and the batch as a whole still has the same 24-hour window. Setting stream to true is not supported in batches, because results come back as one file after processing ends. Streaming belongs to the synchronous Messages API, where it reduces the latency users notice on long interactive runs. For pull request feedback in particular, Claude Code GitHub Actions is the documented way to run reviews on pull_request events in real time.

Read the full guidance on when batches fit and their completion behavior at Message Batches, and compare it with the synchronous request model in Working with Messages.

QUESTION: The reviewer kept flagging intentionally empty catch blocks that carry a best-effort cleanup comment. The team added few-shot examples marking that idiom acceptable, and now the reviewer also ignores catch blocks that silently swallow real errors. How should the examples be revised?
answers: Keep the examples and ask the reviewer to attach a self-rated confidence score to each finding.
Remove the examples and instruct the reviewer to flag every empty catch block as a bug.
Add more examples of the accepted idiom so the pattern is learned more firmly.
Pair each acceptable idiom with a similar-looking genuine defect, stating why only one is reportable.
feedbacks: Self-rated confidence does not fix the wrong judgment. If the reviewer has learned to treat a swallowed error (an error that is caught and then ignored) as acceptable, that error never becomes a finding, so there is nothing to score. Confidence notes can help sort findings that exist, but they cannot bring back issues that the examples taught the model to skip.

A rule that flags every empty catch block brings back the original false positives on the intentional cleanup pattern. That is what developers complained about at the start. It replaces one wrong calibration with the opposite one, instead of teaching the judgment that separates the two cases.

Adding more examples of the same acceptable case makes the overgeneralization the team sees even stronger, because every example says the same thing: empty catch blocks are fine. More examples do not provide the missing information, which is what makes a case that looks similar a real issue.

Contrasting pairs teach where the decision boundary is, not a pattern of how the code looks. The model learns that an empty catch is acceptable when the comment documents an intentional best-effort cleanup, and reportable when a real error is dropped. Including the reasoning lets the reviewer apply that distinction to variants that do not look the same as the examples.
prompt.explanation:
Few-shot examples work because they pass on judgment, not only patterns. When every example in a prompt says the same thing (an empty catch block with a comment is acceptable), the model has no information about where that acceptance ends. So it applies the lesson to any block that looks similar, including blocks that silently discard real failures. That is the failure in this scenario. The examples did remove the false positives, but they created false negatives, because they showed only one side of the boundary.

The fix is to make the examples contrastive. Place each accepted pattern next to a real defect that looks almost the same, and explain why each one is or is not reportable. The cleanup block is acceptable because the comment documents an intentional best-effort decision and nothing later in the code depends on the failure. The swallowed exception is a bug because callers continue as if the operation succeeded. Anthropic's guidance on examples says they should be diverse enough to cover edge cases and to avoid teaching unintended patterns. Its classification guides recommend giving both cases that should be flagged and cases that should not, with the reasoning, so the model can apply the logic to inputs it has never seen. Two to four such pairs usually do more than a dozen examples that show only one side.

Each of the other approaches misses the boundary problem. Adding more examples of the accepted pattern makes the overgeneralization stronger. Going back to a rule that flags every empty catch block only replaces the false negatives with the original false positives. Attaching self-rated confidence to findings can help developers sort them faster. But a case that the reviewer has been taught to consider fine never appears as a finding at all, so there is nothing for the confidence score to describe. Precision and recall in a code reviewer depend on whether the model can tell an accepted convention from a defect. Contrasting examples with reasoning are the mechanism that teaches that distinction.

See Claude prompting best practices and the content moderation guide for guidance on diverse, edge-case examples that include both flagged and allowed cases.

QUESTION: A developer on this team used plan mode to address a CI finding that test fixtures are duplicated across 40 modules; Claude proposed a shared fixture design the developer agrees with. What should happen next?
answers: Copy the fixture design into the project CLAUDE.md so future sessions apply it automatically.
Stay in plan mode and instruct Claude to begin editing each module listed in the plan.
Approve the plan so the session leaves plan mode and Claude implements the agreed design.
Open a fresh session and paste the plan text as the opening implementation prompt.
feedbacks: CLAUDE.md holds universal conventions that always load. It does not hold the implementation steps for one refactor. Putting a one-time task plan there adds permanent context to every session, and the current refactor still does not get done.

While a session is in plan mode, Claude is instructed to research and propose changes instead of editing. Under normal plan-mode permissions, edits stay blocked until a plan is approved. The developer would be asking for implementation in a mode whose purpose is to delay implementation until the design has been approved.

Plan mode exists to separate design from execution. Under normal plan-mode permissions, Claude explores and proposes changes without editing, and implementation waits for an approved plan. Approving the plan is the documented step that leaves plan mode and enters the selected permission mode for implementation. Because work continues in the same session, Claude normally keeps the knowledge about dependencies and structure that it gathered while planning. The exception is when the developer chooses or configures an approval option that clears the planning context.

A new session starts without any of the codebase knowledge that Claude built while exploring the 40 modules. So Claude must discover the dependencies again, even though the plan already accounts for them. This throws away the main benefit of planning first and makes likely the extra rework that plan mode is meant to prevent.
prompt.explanation:
Plan mode is a Claude Code permission mode, not a separate model. In plan mode, Claude can read files and run exploratory commands, and it is instructed to research and propose changes instead of making them. Under normal plan-mode permissions, edits stay blocked until the user approves the plan. (The documented exception is an interactive terminal session where bypass permissions are available, which is not the situation in this scenario.) This design makes the expensive part of a large change, the design decisions, cheap to revise. Changing a written plan takes a few minutes. Cleaning up after a 40-module refactor that went in the wrong direction can take hours. So the documented workflow has two phases: plan first and approve, then execute.

Approving the plan is the step that connects those two phases. When Claude presents a plan, the developer can approve it or keep planning. When approving, the developer chooses whether auto mode runs the edits or whether each edit is reviewed by hand. After approval, the session switches to the selected permission mode and Claude starts implementing. Implementation continues in the same session, so it normally keeps the planning conversation and what Claude learned about the modules, their imports and their existing fixtures. The exception is when the developer chooses or configures an approval option that clears the planning context before implementation starts. In the default flow, this kept context is what makes the implementation consistent with the design.

Asking Claude to start editing while still in plan mode works against the purpose of the mode. Claude is instructed to plan without editing, and under normal plan-mode permissions the edits are blocked anyway. So the request delays implementation instead of starting it. Starting a new session with the plan pasted in does allow implementation. But it throws away the exploration context and forces Claude to work out again the dependencies that the plan already resolved. That is the rework the planning phase was meant to avoid. CLAUDE.md is the wrong place for a one-time task. It holds conventions that should apply to every session. Loading a refactor plan into every future conversation adds noise, and it does not carry out the change.

In this team's CI setup, the pipeline itself runs non-interactively with -p. So plan mode is for the developer who acts on CI findings locally, where a human is present to review and approve the plan. See Permission modes for the plan mode approval flow and Commands for the /plan command.

QUESTION: A CI job asks Claude to return test-case suggestions for each pull request as JSON in the response text. The pipeline step that posts the PR comment sometimes rejects the output as malformed or missing a required field. Which change most reliably eliminates these rejections?
answers: Rewrite the instruction to demand complete, valid JSON only, listing every required field and forbidding any commentary.
Wrap the comment-posting step in a retry loop that re-sends the diff whenever it rejects the payload as malformed or incomplete.
Define a test-suggestion tool with "strict" set to true whose input schema is the payload structure, and read the "tool_use" input.
Add a post-processing stage that repairs malformed JSON with a lenient parser and fills missing fields with default values.
feedbacks: Stronger wording makes success more likely, but the output stays in free text, where the model can still leave out a field or make a syntax error. Prompt instructions alone give probabilistic compliance, not a structural guarantee.

Retrying generates the same kind of free-text output again. It will often succeed in the end, but it adds latency and cost to a step that developers wait for, and it never removes the cause of the failure. A retry loop treats the symptom, while the output channel stays unreliable.

Declaring the payload structure as a strict tool input schema moves the output out of free text. The tool input is produced with grammar-constrained sampling, which guarantees that it matches the schema, including required fields and types. The pipeline reads the suggestion data directly from the tool_use block, so malformed syntax and missing keys never reach the step that posts the comment.

Lenient repair and filling in default values are fragile workarounds based on guessing. They fix only the failures seen so far, and they silently invent data for fields the model left out. Building a custom repair layer is unnecessary when a documented mechanism already produces output that matches the schema.
prompt.explanation:
The rejections in this pipeline all have the same cause. The test-case suggestions are carried inside Claude's free-text response, and in free text the model is allowed to add extra words, stop early, or leave parts out. Clever parsing cannot change that. The reliable fix is to change the channel. Declare the payload structure as a tool's input_schema and mark the tool strict: true. Claude then gives its suggestions as a tool_use block. The input of that block is produced with grammar-constrained sampling and is guaranteed to match the schema, so required fields are present and types are correct. The CI job reads the fields from the block. The pipeline never executes anything. The tool exists only so that the output arrives in a typed structure instead of as plain text that happens to contain JSON.

The methods for getting structured output can be ranked by reliability. The least reliable is a plain instruction to "return JSON". Next is prefilling the assistant turn with an opening brace. Next is describing the schema in the prompt. Next is an ordinary tool with an input schema: Claude is trained to follow it, but it can still leave out a required field or use an incompatible type. The most reliable is strict tool use, which enforces the schema at decoding time. Each step up gives up a little flexibility and gains a lot of determinism. For a program that consumes the output, like the step that posts the PR comment, you want the most reliable method. Anthropic's current docs give the same guarantee for a final JSON response through output_config.format, for cases where the result should be a fixed JSON reply instead of a tool call. The two mechanisms can be used separately or together. Both compile the schema into a grammar. This adds a little latency on first use and limits which JSON Schema features are supported. Unsupported constructs, such as recursive schemas or numeric bounds, are rejected instead of being silently ignored.

It is important to be clear about what this provides. Strict tool use removes syntax and shape errors: the braces close, required keys appear and types match. It does not check the facts in the semantic content. A suggestion can still name a scenario that the existing suite already covers, or point at the wrong file. So validation logic for business rules is still needed. The docs also note edge cases where even structured output is not delivered, such as a refusal or a response cut off at max_tokens. So the pipeline should still check stop_reason.

The other approaches fail for related reasons. Stricter prompt wording only makes clean text more likely. A retry loop only tries again and hopes for a different result, and it adds latency to a check that blocks developers. A custom repair layer that fills missing fields with defaults invents data instead of preventing the missing fields. See Strict tool use, Structured outputs, and How tool use works.

QUESTION: The team's system prompt tells the agent to "search for relevant context before answering." A connected MCP server exposes a "search_tickets" tool, and logs show the agent calling it for code questions instead of Grep. Which TWO changes most directly fix this misrouting? (Select TWO.)
answers: Reword the instruction to name the intended behavior, such as using Grep to find code, instead of a generic "search" directive.
Add boundary language to the "search_tickets" description stating that it covers issue tracker tickets only, not source code.
Set "tool_choice" to "any" so the agent is guaranteed to invoke some tool before answering any code question.
Add a capitalized rule stating the agent MUST NEVER call "search_tickets" unless the user explicitly references a ticket number.
feedbacks: The general verb "search" in the system prompt matches the name of the "search_tickets" tool. This pushes the model toward that tool whenever the instruction applies. Naming the intended behavior concretely (find relevant code with Grep) removes the accidental word association at its source.

Tool descriptions are the main signal the model uses when it chooses among tools. The documented fix for calls to the wrong tool is to make clear when to use each tool. Stating that "search_tickets" is for issue tracker tickets and not for source code gives the model a clear reason not to use it for code questions.

The "any" setting only guarantees that some tool is called. It says nothing about which tool. The agent already calls a tool in this scenario, just the wrong one. So forcing tool use addresses a completely different problem.

Anthropic specifically recommends against forceful wording such as MUST or NEVER, because it distorts when tools are triggered on current models. This rule would also block real ticket lookups that do not mention a ticket number. It also keeps the ambiguous "search" instruction, so the underlying association does not change.
prompt.explanation:
Claude selects a tool by matching the request, as the system prompt frames it, to each tool's described capability. This matching is based on meaning, not on a strict keyword match. But the words in the prompt, the tool names and the tool descriptions all affect it. When a system prompt uses a broad verb such as search, and one of the available tools is literally named search_tickets, the instruction and the tool name strengthen each other. The model can then use the ticket tool for code exploration, where Grep was intended. This is the mechanism that the scenario tests. Wording in the system prompt creates associations with tools whose names use the same words, even when nobody intended that link.

The two changes that fix this directly work on the two sides of the association. Rewording the instruction to describe the behavior concretely (use Grep to find relevant code) removes the ambiguous trigger word. Adding boundary language to the search_tickets description (issue tracker tickets, not source code) gives the model a documented reason to exclude that tool for code questions. Anthropic's troubleshooting guidance for calls to the wrong tool says to distinguish tools by when to use them, not only by what they do. This applies in the same way to MCP tools that are available next to built-in tools. When their wording overlaps, the agent may otherwise treat them as interchangeable.

The remaining approaches miss the mechanism. A capitalized MUST NEVER rule is the kind of forceful wording that Anthropic now advises replacing with plain phrasing such as "Use this tool when...". On current models, aggressive language tends to make tool triggering overcorrect, so tools are triggered too often. In this case, it would also block real ticket lookups that are phrased without a ticket number, and the ambiguous instruction would stay. Setting tool_choice to any controls whether a tool is called, not which one. So it cannot help when the agent already calls tools and only chooses the wrong one. Teams that combine built-in tools with MCP servers should check the wording of their prompts against tool names and descriptions. They should fix selection problems in the descriptions and instructions before they try stronger enforcement.

See Troubleshooting tool use, Claude prompting best practices, and Define tools.

QUESTION: The team's /scaffold-module skill creates several boilerplate files on each invocation. Developers are interrupted by a permission prompt for every file write. They want file writes approved without a prompt, but only while this skill runs. What should the team change?
answers: Add an "allowed-tools" entry listing Write to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter.
Invoke the skill in plan mode so the file writes proceed without prompts.
State in the skill's instructions that file writes are pre-approved and need no confirmation.
Add Write to "permissions.allow" in the project's .claude/settings.json file.
feedbacks: The allowed-tools field in the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) pre-approves the listed tools for the turn in which the skill is invoked. So Write runs without a prompt while the skill runs. Bash is not listed, so it stays under the normal permission settings and still prompts. The approval ends when the user sends the next message.

Plan mode is read-only. In plan mode, Claude investigates and proposes changes, but it does not edit or create files. A scaffolding skill must write boilerplate files, so it cannot do its job in that mode. This option changes the workflow but does not solve the prompt problem.

Claude Code itself enforces permission rules. The model does not enforce them by reading instructions. Text in a skill body or in CLAUDE.md cannot grant or remove tool access, so the prompts would continue as before.

A permissions.allow rule pre-approves Write for every prompt in every session, not only while the skill runs. It removes the write prompt everywhere. That is broader than the team asked for, and it removes the review step for ordinary edits.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code keeps two things separate: what a skill instructs Claude to do, and what Claude Code permits a tool to do. Skill content is guidance. Permission rules are enforced by the harness, whatever the model wants. The allowed-tools field in SKILL.md frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) belongs to the permission side. It pre-approves the listed tools so that Claude can call them without prompting during the turn that invokes the skill. You can write the list as a YAML list or as a space- or comma-separated string. It uses the same ToolName or ToolName(specifier) syntax as permission rules. If a scaffolding skill lists Write, the boilerplate files are created without a confirmation for each file. Bash is not listed, so it is still controlled by the user's normal permission settings and prompts as before.

Two limits matter when you reason about this field. First, the approval is turn-scoped. It applies while the turn that invoked the skill runs, and it ends when the user sends the next message, even if the skill's content is still in context. Invoking the skill again applies it again. Second, allowed-tools does not remove other tools from Claude's set of tools. It only adds pre-approval for the tools it lists. If a team needs a tool removed while a skill is active, the frontmatter field for that is disallowed-tools. To block a tool across all prompts and skills, the right place is permissions.deny in settings. Also note that a project skill's allowed-tools is honored even in an untrusted folder. So the team should review checked-in skills before running Claude Code in a new repository.

Each of the other approaches fails. A permissions.allow rule in .claude/settings.json is the right tool for session-wide pre-approval. In this case, though, it would stop write prompts for every task, not only for the scaffolding workflow. Writing "no confirmation needed" into the skill's instructions does nothing, because prompt text cannot grant tool access. Plan mode is read-only by design, so a skill whose purpose is to create files cannot run in it. See Claude Code Skills for the frontmatter fields and Claude Code Permissions for how allow and deny rules are enforced.

QUESTION: A team wants the agent to read GitHub issues and pull requests, and also to query an internal on-call catalog, a service with a proprietary HTTP API that lists the on-call owner of each microservice. A developer proposes writing custom MCP servers for both. What should the team do instead?
answers: Use an existing GitHub MCP server and build a custom MCP server only for the internal on-call catalog.
Postpone both integrations until the Anthropic Directory lists a reviewed connector for each system.
Have the agent call the GitHub REST API through Bash with curl instead of connecting any MCP server.
Build custom MCP servers for both systems so the team fully controls tool names and descriptions.
feedbacks: GitHub is a standard integration. Well-established MCP servers and connectors already exist for it, so reusing one avoids building and maintaining a duplicate. The on-call catalog is a system specific to this team, behind a proprietary API. That is the case where a custom MCP server is justified.

An internal catalog behind a proprietary API is unlikely to become available as a public connector. Waiting for a directory listing would stop the team's work with no benefit. A directory listing affects whether a connector can be found and whether it has been reviewed. A custom or private MCP server that the team adds itself is a fully supported option for systems like this.

If the agent works with GitHub through improvised shell commands, it has no tool descriptions or input schemas to choose from. It also gets no MCP-style tool results to recover with. MCP exists to provide those contracts. An existing GitHub server gives the agent a described tool interface without any custom code.

A custom server for GitHub repeats work that existing servers already do. It also adds ongoing maintenance for a common, standard integration. Custom servers are the right choice only for workflows that are unique to the team, not for standard services.
prompt.explanation:
The main principle for MCP integration work is to reuse existing servers for standard integrations and to build custom servers only for workflows unique to the team. GitHub, Jira, Slack, and similar services already have MCP servers and connectors. In Claude Code, the team adds the chosen GitHub server directly. It can be a remote server listed in the Anthropic Directory, or any other existing server the team selects. The team registers it with claude mcp add or declares it in the project's .mcp.json. When Claude Code connects to the server, it discovers the server's tools automatically. The existing server already contains the tool descriptions and input schemas that the team would otherwise have to design, test, and keep in sync with the upstream API. A second GitHub server would give the team little more than control over tool names. It would also cost real maintenance effort every time the API changes.

The on-call catalog is a different kind of case. It is a private system with a proprietary HTTP API, so it is unlikely to be available as a public connector. A custom MCP server is the appropriate way to give the agent a clear, described tool for it. Custom servers are a fully supported option in Claude's connector model. They are added by URL (or run locally for Claude Code) without Anthropic review. They run on the same MCP runtime as directory connectors. The documentation recommends them for private or tenant-specific systems. The team can configure both servers in the project's .mcp.json and supply any tokens through environment variable expansion. Then the whole team gets the same tools from version control.

The other approaches each put the effort in the wrong place. Building both servers themselves treats a common, standard integration as if it were a custom one. Reaching GitHub through curl in Bash throws away the structured interface that makes tool selection reliable, and an existing server provides that interface without extra work. Waiting for a directory listing for an internal system confuses discoverability with capability. The directory decides whether other users can find a connector. It does not decide whether the team can connect a server that it hosts itself. One caution applies when the team reuses a server. Within the Anthropic Directory, a connector labeled Community has been screened, but Anthropic has not reviewed it in depth. A server taken from GitHub or another registry has no Anthropic screening at all. So the team should evaluate whichever GitHub server it adopts and give it only the access it needs.

See Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP, Directory vs custom connectors, and Connector verification.

QUESTION: An engineer wants this agent to add caching to a poorly understood legacy service. The agent's tools list contains only "Read", "Grep", "Glob", and "Write". Which TWO steps let the agent use the interview pattern before implementation? (Select TWO.)
answers: Delegate the questioning to a subagent spawned through the Agent tool so the main context stays uncluttered.
Prompt the agent to question the engineer about invalidation rules, failure modes, and tradeoffs before it writes code.
Add "AskUserQuestion" to the agent's tools list so its clarifying questions can actually reach the engineer.
Have the agent rate its own confidence in a design and ask questions only when that score falls below a threshold.
feedbacks: AskUserQuestion is not available in subagents spawned through the Agent tool. So a subagent cannot send questions back to the engineer. Subagents do give a real benefit of context isolation for verbose exploration. But they are the wrong mechanism for a conversation that must reach a human.

This is the core of the interview pattern. Claude asks about the hard parts, such as edge cases, failure modes, and tradeoffs. That way, issues the engineer has not thought about come up before any implementation starts. In an unfamiliar legacy service, cache invalidation and failure behavior are the kind of design decisions that a direct prompt would guess at without telling anyone.

In the Agent SDK, Claude asks clarifying questions through the built-in AskUserQuestion tool. The application receives those questions through the canUseTool callback and shows them to the user. When an explicit tools list leaves this tool out, Claude has no way to interview the engineer. The pattern then cannot work, however the prompt is written.

Self-rated confidence is unreliable, because the model can be confident and wrong. This is especially true in an unfamiliar domain, where the model does not know what it does not know. The interview pattern asks questions at the start on purpose. It does not make the questions depend on a self-assessment.
prompt.explanation:
The interview pattern is documented as "Let Claude interview you". It reverses the usual direction of prompting for larger or uncertain pieces of work. The engineer does not try to write a complete specification from memory. Instead, Claude gets a minimal prompt and is asked to interview the engineer about technical implementation, edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs. Claude asks in detail about the parts the engineer may not have considered. For a caching layer on a legacy service, those parts are usually invalidation rules, behavior when the cache is unavailable, and consistency expectations. A direct prompt would make the agent guess at each one. Anthropic recommends that Claude write the result to a spec such as SPEC.md. The implementation then starts from that spec in a fresh session, so the implementation context stays focused.

In an Agent SDK application, the pattern depends on a mechanism that is easy to miss. Claude asks its questions through the built-in AskUserQuestion tool. The application receives them through the canUseTool callback, shows the generated multiple-choice questions, and returns the engineer's selections. AskUserQuestion is available by default. But when the agent is configured with an explicit tools array (in this case only Read, Grep, Glob, and Write), the tool must be listed explicitly, or Claude cannot ask. So two steps together make the pattern work: prompt the agent to interview, and make sure the question tool is available.

The other approaches fail for different reasons. Subagents spawned through the Agent tool are valuable for keeping verbose discovery output out of the main context. But AskUserQuestion is not available inside them, so a subagent that does the interview has no way to reach the engineer. A rule that asks questions only when a self-rated confidence score is low depends on the model knowing the limits of its own knowledge. That knowledge is what is missing in an unfamiliar domain. The interview pattern always asks, and does not trust that self-assessment. Note that this extra effort is justified when the approach is uncertain, the change spans many files, or the code is unfamiliar. For a small fix with a clear scope, asking the agent to do the task directly is still the right choice.

See Claude Code best practices for the interview workflow and Agent SDK user input for how AskUserQuestion is shown to the user and what its limitations are.

QUESTION: The team connects an MCP server whose "search_symbols" tool searches a prebuilt index of dozens of repositories, but the tool's description says only "Searches code." The agent nearly always uses Grep instead, missing matches outside the current checkout. What should the team change first?
answers: Add a system prompt rule instructing the agent to always call "search_symbols" before falling back to Grep for any code search task.
Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools so that "search_symbols" becomes the only available way to search code across the repositories.
Rewrite the "search_symbols" description to state what it returns, when to use it instead of Grep, and its cross-repository coverage.
Rename the tool to "grep_symbols" so the agent associates it with the Grep behavior it already selects reliably.
feedbacks: A system prompt rule that applies to every search is weaker and probabilistic. It is also far from the place where tool selection actually happens. The rule forces the index tool even for local, single-file searches where Grep is the right choice. The description itself stays uninformative, so the real ambiguity remains.

Removing Grep seriously limits the agent's ability to explore the checked-out code step by step, which is a core task for this system. It forces a choice by removing a capability. It does not give the model the information it needs to choose correctly.

Tool descriptions are the main signal the model uses to choose among tools. A two-word description gives the model no reason to prefer the MCP tool over a familiar built-in tool. The new description should say what the index returns, when to choose it over Grep, and which cross-repository data only this tool can reach. That fixes the root cause of the wrong tool choice.

Names are a weaker signal than descriptions. Making the MCP tool look more like Grep increases the overlap between the two tools instead of removing it. A tool with an easily confused name and no explanation of when to use it will be selected less reliably, not more.
prompt.explanation:
When a request includes tools, the tool definitions are placed into a tool-use system prompt. Claude decides which tool to call based on the request and on each tool's description. Anthropic says detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance. It recommends at least three to four sentences that cover what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what its parameters mean, and any caveats. A description such as "Searches code" is a standard example of a poor description. It tells the model nothing about the prebuilt index, the repositories it covers, or how it differs from Grep.

This scenario has a specific detail that comes up often in Agent SDK and Claude Code work. An agent that already has built-in tools like Grep tends to prefer them over MCP tools that seem to do the same thing. The fix is to make the MCP tool's description stronger. It should point out the concrete advantage that the built-in tool cannot provide, which in this case is symbol lookup across repositories beyond the current checkout. It should also say plainly when to choose the tool. Anthropic's troubleshooting guidance makes the same point. When the model selects the wrong tool, the cause is usually an ambiguous description. The fix is to distinguish the tools by saying when to use each one, not only what each one does.

The other approaches avoid the problem instead of fixing it. A system prompt rule to always try search_symbols first is a probabilistic instruction. It also sends local searches, which Grep handles best, to the wrong tool. Removing Grep forces the choice by deleting a capability that the agent needs to explore the checked-out code step by step. Renaming the tool to look like Grep makes the two tools easier to confuse. Names carry less weight than descriptions, and this overlap is what causes the wrong selection.

See Define tools, Troubleshooting tool use, and Claude Code MCP for details.

QUESTION: A developer defines "codebase-explorer" and "boilerplate-writer" subagents with "AgentDefinition" and sets the coordinator's "allowedTools" to Read, Grep, Glob, and Bash. In unattended runs where unlisted tools are denied, the coordinator never delegates and explores everything itself. What change enables delegation?
answers: Register each subagent as an MCP server in ".mcp.json" so it appears in the coordinator's tool list.
Add "Task" (named "Agent" in current SDK versions) to the coordinator's "allowedTools" list.
Add "Task" to each subagent's "tools" field so the subagents can accept delegated work.
Rewrite the coordinator's system prompt to explicitly instruct it to delegate exploration to the subagents.
feedbacks: MCP servers expose external tools and resources. They are not the mechanism for defining or invoking SDK subagents. These subagents are already defined through AgentDefinition, and they are spawned through the subagent tool. Wrapping them as MCP servers adds unneeded extra code for a problem that one allowed-tools entry solves.

Subagents are spawned through the Task tool, which is shown as Agent in current SDK releases. So the coordinator can delegate only when that tool is approved for it. In this unattended setup, unlisted tools are denied. Every spawn attempt is rejected until the tool appears in the coordinator's allowed tools. That is why defining the subagents alone changed nothing.

A subagent's tools field controls what that subagent can call once it is running. It does not control whether the coordinator may spawn it. The parent starts the delegation. So giving the subagents the spawning tool leaves the coordinator as blocked as before.

Prompt wording can encourage delegation, but it cannot make a denied tool usable. The coordinator may try to delegate, but the permission setup rejects each spawn call. So the prompt change does not fix the real cause of the block.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a coordinator does not call subagents directly. It makes a tool call to the subagent-spawning tool. This tool was historically named Task and is shown as Agent in current SDK releases. Older versions still report Task, so detection code often matches both names. Defining subagents with AgentDefinition tells Claude what each one does and when to use it. But the spawn itself is just another tool use. It goes through the same permission handling as Read or Bash. Delegation is a tool call, and if the harness refuses that tool call, no subagent is created.

The allowedTools list is the auto-approval list. Tools on it run without prompting. Tools not on it are passed to the permission mode and any permission callback. In an interactive session, a missing entry might show up as a prompt. In the unattended configuration in this question, unlisted tools are denied. If the subagent tool is left out, every delegation attempt is rejected automatically, without asking anyone to approve it. The coordinator then does all the exploration in its own context. This removes the context-isolation benefit that subagents exist to provide. The direct fix is to add the subagent tool to the coordinator's allowed tools, next to the built-in tools it already has.

Each incorrect approach targets the wrong layer. A subagent's own tools field limits what that subagent can do after it starts. Putting the spawning tool there does nothing for the parent. Stronger prompt instructions are probabilistic guidance. They cannot override a deterministic permission denial. MCP servers are the integration method for external systems such as issue trackers or documentation stores. They are not a way to expose SDK subagents. Registering the subagents there again adds extra machinery and does not fix the missing permission.

See Subagents in the SDK for how subagents are invoked through the Agent tool (and the legacy Task naming), and Agent SDK permissions for how allowedTools works with permission modes and callbacks.

QUESTION: A PreToolUse hook matching the agent's migration tool denies every call, enforcing the rule that production migrations must be handed to a DBA. The tool's "target" argument chooses between production and staging, and staging migrations are now blocked too. How should the hook be corrected?
answers: Remove the hook and add a project CLAUDE.md rule stating that the migration tool may only be called with a staging or development target, never production.
Change the hook to run asynchronously so it records production attempts for later audit while staging and development migrations proceed without interruption.
Keep the matcher on the migration tool and inspect the "target" value in "tool_input", denying with a reason that names the DBA handoff only when the target is production.
Replace the matcher with a pattern that includes the environment, such as "mcp__dbops__run_migration:production", so the hook fires only on production calls and ignores staging.
feedbacks: CLAUDE.md is guidance that the model usually follows. It is not code that runs on every tool call. For this rule, a single violation means a production migration that nobody reviewed. When a deterministic hook is available, probabilistic compliance is not acceptable for a rule like that.

When a hook runs asynchronously, the agent continues immediately. So the hook cannot block, change, or redirect a tool call. That makes it suitable only for logging or metrics. It cannot stop a production migration from running.

Matchers select hooks by tool name only. So the environment check must happen inside the hook, by reading the tool input. For production targets, the hook returns a deny decision with a reason. This blocks the call before it runs and tells Claude to send the work to the DBA. Staging and development calls continue normally.

Hook matchers filter on the tool name. They do not filter on argument values such as an environment or an amount. A matcher string that includes the target would never match the real tool name. The policy would then stop being enforced for every environment, and nothing would report it.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, the agent loop runs whatever tool call the model produces. So the place to stop an action before it has side effects is a PreToolUse hook. The hook fires after Claude has chosen the tool and built its arguments. It receives tool_name, tool_input, and a tool-use ID. A matcher limits which tool names trigger the hook, but it works on the name alone. Any decision that depends on the arguments, such as an environment name, a refund amount, or a file path, has to be made in the hook body by reading tool_input. The original deny-all hook used the correct event and the correct matcher. But it skipped that inspection step, and that is why it also blocked staging migrations.

The fix keeps the matcher on the migration tool and checks the target field. For production, the hook returns a permissionDecision of deny with a permissionDecisionReason such as "production migrations are run by a DBA; hand off the migration file". For every other target, it returns allow or makes no decision, so the call continues through the normal permission flow. Claude sees the reason text. This turns a plain block into a redirection. The model learns why the call failed, and it can continue by preparing the handoff instead of retrying the same call. A hook denial also takes priority over any more permissive signal. Resuming is the right choice only when the earlier context can still be trusted. In this case, the restored history contains file contents and search results that the refactor has made invalid. So the agent starts with confident but wrong knowledge about where the code is.

Resuming restores that transcript as it was. It does not take a snapshot of the filesystem or check it again. If the files the agent read last week have been moved and renamed, the restored Read and Grep results describe a codebase that no longer exists. The agent will reason from them with full confidence, because nothing in the transcript tells it they are wrong.

The decision rule is: resume when the earlier context can still be trusted, and start fresh with an injected summary when earlier tool results are outdated. Starting fresh does not mean throwing away the work. The engineer keeps the results that are still valid (the dependency map, the decisions made, the open questions). The engineer puts them as a short structured block in the new session's first prompt, and adds a clear note such as "these files were moved or renamed since the analysis". The agent then re-reads only the affected files instead of doing the whole exploration again. Anthropic's own guidance for work across hosts and for long-running work recommends the same pattern. It is a tool for keeping a long conversation inside the context window. A summary of outdated findings is a smaller set of outdated findings. When the main agent spawns a standard subagent, that subagent's context window starts fresh. It receives its own system prompt, the delegation prompt, and environment details such as CLAUDE.md. It does not receive the parent's system prompt, the parent's conversation history, or the files the parent already read. Only its final message comes back to the main agent. This design tradeoff is what makes subagents valuable for exploring a codebase. Verbose discovery output stays out of the main conversation, but the parent never sees the raw evidence. So a subagent prompt should ask for the concrete artifacts that the coordinator will need, such as file paths, line references, and call chains, because the parent cannot go back and inspect what the subagent saw.
