Tools that remain in the subagent's tool set tend to get used, and the logs already show this behavior. The fix belongs in the tool configuration, not in instructions.

The parent's allowedTools option controls which tools are auto-approved without a permission prompt. It is not a restriction for each subagent, and it does not remove other tools from a subagent's tool set. The real mechanism for limiting a subagent's tools is the tools or disallowedTools field inside that subagent's own AgentDefinition.

The disallowedTools field removes tools from a subagent's tool set. It supports MCP server-level patterns such as mcp__github__*, which removes every tool from that server. The boilerplate generator then cannot reach the GitHub tools at all. This stops the subagent from using tools that belong to another role, and the configuration enforces it.

The tools field in an AgentDefinition is an allowlist for that subagent. When it is set, any tool that is not listed does not exist in the subagent's session. Limiting the explorer to Read, Grep, and Glob makes writing files impossible, not only discouraged. This is the scoped tool access pattern for subagents with specific roles.

In the Claude Agent SDK, each subagent is described by an AgentDefinition. It contains the subagent's description, system prompt, and tool restrictions. A subagent's set of tools is fixed when it is defined. It is not decided at runtime. If the tools field is left out, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents. If the field is present, it works as an allowlist, and anything not listed does not exist in that subagent's session. A missing tool causes no permission prompt and no runtime error. The model never sees it. That is why limiting the exploration subagent to Read, Grep, and Glob is a structural fix. This design choice is deliberate. Agents choose more reliably from a small set of tools that fit their role than from a full catalog. Tools outside a role tend to be misused because they are available.

The second field, disallowedTools, removes tools from the inherited set instead of listing the allowed ones, and it understands MCP naming. MCP tools have standard names of the form mcp__SERVER__TOOL. So a pattern such as mcp__github__* removes every tool that one server exposes. That makes it the natural way to stop a boilerplate generator from calling a GitHub integration it has no reason to use. The server stays available to subagents that do need it.

The incorrect approaches fail for different reasons. A system prompt rule that lists forbidden tools leaves those tools in the subagent's tool set. It depends on the model following the instruction every time. Prompts influence what Claude tries to do, but they do not grant or remove access. The restriction for each subagent exists only inside the agent definition.

The SDK permits nested subagent spawning. But if one spoke decides whether the others run, the routing decision moves out of the coordinator. That fits the hub-and-spoke pattern less well than keeping the selection at the hub. It also makes the other subagents wait for the first one's findings, one after another. The coordinator could instead run them in parallel when both are needed.

prompt.explanation:
In a hub-and-spoke architecture, the coordinator is the component that first receives the full request. It is responsible for deciding what context to pass to each spoke. So it is the natural place, and the designed place, to decide which spokes a request needs. The Claude Agent SDK documentation says that the main agent uses each subagent's description to decide when to delegate. It also says that subagents exist for focused subtasks: context isolation, parallel analyses, specialized instructions, and tool restrictions. Spawning every subagent on every request loses those benefits, because each spawn is a separate agent instance with its own fresh context and its own model calls. The fix that keeps the pattern intact is to make the selection dynamic at the hub. The coordinator reads the request and picks the subagents that can help. It delegates to those subagents (in parallel when they are independent) and combines the results.

This decision belongs at the coordinator, not in the spokes, because of what each part can see. A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context window. It does not inherit the parent conversation history or the parent's tool results. So any file paths, constraints, or decisions it needs must be included explicitly in the delegation prompt. Its own intermediate work stays inside its context, and only the final report goes back to the parent. If you ask a subagent to judge whether it is relevant, you pay for a fresh instance and an inference only to receive "nothing to do". The SDK allows one subagent to spawn the others. Nesting is limited by a default depth limit, not forbidden. But this moves the selection decision from the hub into a spoke. The nested delegation happens inside the first subagent's own context, not at the coordinator, where the pattern expects routing and aggregation to happen. The later subagents also have to wait for the first one instead of running at the same time. Combining the three into one general-purpose explorer removes the specialized instructions and the tool limits for each subagent, which make each spoke predictable. It also does nothing about the routing problem, because the single large subagent would still run for every question.

In practice, the coordinator does three jobs in one place. At the start, it breaks the request into parts and selects subagents. It passes the needed context explicitly to each spoke. At the end, it combines the results and handles errors. Keeping all three jobs at the hub gives you observability and one consistent way to recover from errors. If any of these jobs moves into the spokes, the system becomes harder to understand and debug than the pattern intends. Return the summary in "updatedToolOutput" so it replaces what the model receives.
Return the summary in "additionalContext" so it is attached to the tool result.

For a PostToolUse hook, the documented way to rewrite a tool result before Claude sees it is the updatedToolOutput field. A block decision only adds the reason next to the original result, and that is the behavior the team observed. If the hook uses updatedToolOutput instead, Claude receives the short summary in place of the raw output.

The additionalContext field adds information next to the tool result. It does not replace the result. The model would still receive the full raw test output plus the summary, so this does not solve the problem.

Asynchronous hook output is only for side effects. When a hook runs in async mode, the agent continues without waiting. So the hook cannot change the tool result or add anything to the current operation.
prompt.explanation:
Hooks in the Claude Agent SDK run at fixed points in the agent loop. The model requests a tool, the SDK runs it, and the result goes back to the model for its next decision. A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool runs and before the result goes back to the model. That is why it is the natural place to transform what the model sees. For example, it can trim verbose output, normalize formats, or condense a long log into a summary. The hook is code, not a prompt instruction. So the transformation is applied every time, not only when the model remembers to ignore noise.

The difficult part is knowing what each output field does. On PostToolUse, updatedToolOutput replaces the tool result before Claude sees it. additionalContext adds text next to the result. decision: "block" does not hide or replace anything. It only attaches the reason next to the original output. A team that uses the block decision and expects it to hide the raw result gets the symptom in this question: the model receives both the raw output and the summary. One more constraint matters for built-in tools. The replacement must match the tool's output shape. For example, Bash output is a structured object with fields such as stdout and stderr. If the shape does not match, the replacement is ignored and the original is kept. MCP tool output is passed through without that schema check.

It also helps to remember the limits of PostToolUse. The command has already run when the hook fires. Any files have already been written and any commands have already run. Telemetry also records the original output before the hook rewrites it. If the goal were to prevent or change the action itself, PreToolUse would be the right event. It is the wrong choice in this question only because there is nothing to summarize before the tool runs. In the same way, an asynchronous hook lets the agent continue without waiting. It can log or send notifications, but it cannot change the current turn or add anything to it.

Using one subagent does avoid repeated reads. But it removes the parallelism that the question asks to keep. It also puts the exploration of the whole codebase into a single context window, which will fill quickly. The modules are independent investigations, and that is the case where the documentation recommends parallel subagents.

That pattern keeps cost low only when the areas do not overlap. In this question, the four module scopes overlap on a shared dependency. So every subagent separately builds the same understanding of the core packages. The coordinator then receives four overlapping summaries that it has to reconcile.

The fix is to divide the scope so that the shared dependency is its own unit of work. The coordinator (or a dedicated subagent it delegates to) explores the core packages once, before the parallel subagents are launched. The summary from that pass then becomes part of every module subagent's delegation prompt. This works because of a central property of subagents. A non-fork subagent starts fresh. It sees none of the parent conversation, none of the files already read, and nothing that another subagent discovered. Anything a subagent needs must be written into its prompt explicitly. When the core-package summary is passed this way, the module subagents can treat the shared code as already understood. They spend their effort only on their assigned module, and the four of them still run at the same time.

A shared file that subagents update and read does not give a reliable order to isolated subagents that run at the same time. It also moves coordination away from the coordinator instead of through it. Putting everything into one sequential subagent removes repeated reads, but it gives up the parallelism that the team wants to keep. Return a successful empty result for zero matches and a response with "isError" set to true for backend failures.

feedbacks: The tool response looks the same in both cases. So the agent cannot know whether the backend was reachable, and any confidence rating would be a guess with no basis. The model's own confidence rating is an unreliable replacement for facts that only the tool can observe and report.

A query that ran and matched nothing is a success. It should be returned as an ordinary empty result. A timeout is an execution failure. It belongs in a response marked with the documented error indicator. When the tool interface separates the two cases, the agent gets a clear signal. It retries outages and accepts real empty results without guessing. Any extra detail about why the call failed, such as a team-defined category or a retryable hint, is custom metadata that the tool may add next to that flag.

This adds retries for every empty result, but the signal still cannot tell the two cases apart. Real empty searches get retried three times. An outage that lasts longer than three attempts still ends with a false "no issues" conclusion. Retry rules in the prompt cannot recover information that the tool never provided.

Marking a successful query with zero matches as an error reports the outcome wrongly. It leads the agent to reword or retry searches that correctly found nothing, with no useful result. The error flag is meant for tool execution failures, not for ordinary results that happen to be empty.
prompt.explanation:
The failure in this scenario is a signal collapse at the tool boundary. Two outcomes need opposite responses (retry or accept), but the tool reports them in the same way. So no amount of reasoning later in the process can tell them apart. The agent is not misbehaving. It is being asked to make a recovery decision without the information that the decision requires.

A tool result answers two separate questions: did the operation run, and what did it find. A search that reaches the tracker and matches nothing ran successfully and found nothing. That is a valid and informative result, and it should be returned as a normal tool result, which may be empty. Anthropic's tool-use documentation shows an empty tool_result as a valid response shape. The web search tool follows the same contract. A successful search with no matches returns an empty content list, and a search that fails returns a separate error object. A timeout, on the other hand, means the operation did not complete. So the tool should report a failure with the documented error indicator: isError on an MCP tool result, or is_error on a Messages API tool_result. Teams often add their own metadata to that error, such as a failure category or a retryable hint. The agent can then retry with backoff or report the outage honestly. Those extra fields are conventions that the application defines on top of the standard error flag. MCP and the Messages API do not define them.

The other approaches all try to make up for missing information instead of providing it. A prompt rule to retry every empty result wastes calls on real empty queries. It still produces a false negative when an outage lasts longer than the allowed number of retries. Marking all empty results as errors reverses the problem. Correct "nothing matched" answers become failures, and the agent investigates them for no reason. Asking the agent to rate its confidence that the backend was reachable asks for a judgment the agent has no basis to make, because the response it sees is the same in both cases. Self-reported confidence cannot replace a real status signal.

QUESTION: This team's MCP server wraps a legacy database and an internal wiki. Traces show the agent spends its first several turns running schema discovery queries and page listings before starting the actual task. Which server change best removes this overhead?
answers: Paste the current schema and wiki page index into the agent system prompt so discovery is unnecessary.
Add a "describe_system" tool that the agent is instructed to call once at the start of each session.
Raise the agent's turn limit so the discovery phase no longer cuts into task execution.
Publish the database schema and wiki page index as MCP resources the agent can read directly.
feedbacks: A static copy of the schema and page index becomes out of date as soon as a table or page changes. The agent would then act on wrong information. It also loads the full inventory into every request, whether or not the task needs it.

This rebuilds the content catalog feature as a custom tool, but the protocol already provides resources for this purpose. It also depends on the agent remembering to make the call. So the discovery step can still be skipped, or repeated in an inconsistent way.
A larger turn budget pays for the exploratory calls instead of removing them. The wasted tool output still builds up in context. The inefficiency stays. It only becomes cheaper to tolerate.

Resources are the MCP primitive for read-oriented data. They tell an agent what exists without taking any actions. When the schema and page index are exposed as resources, a multi-turn exploration phase becomes a direct lookup. The agent starts the task with the information it needs.
prompt.explanation:
The Model Context Protocol separates tools from resources. Tools are model-controlled actions that the agent decides to invoke. Resources are application-driven, read-oriented data such as file contents, database schemas, API documentation, or knowledge-base entries. The difference is roughly like GET versus POST: a tool does something, and a resource describes something. In this scenario, the agent repeatedly queries the information schema or lists wiki pages before it can start real work. It is using actions to rebuild information that could have been published as a content catalog.

A server that supports resources advertises the resources capability. It exposes its catalog through resources/list, which returns descriptors with a uri, a name, and an optional description and mimeType. The actual content is fetched separately with resources/read. Parameterized catalogs, such as one entry per table or per wiki section, can be exposed as resource templates. In Claude Code, the same catalog appears through @ mentions. Resources from connected servers are listed next to files and are fetched into context as attachments. So the data arrives without any exploratory tool call. For the developer productivity agent, publishing the schema and page index as resources means that the first turn of a task already has the overview it needs.

Each of the other approaches fails in a recognizable way. A dedicated describe_system tool builds again what resources already provide. Because it is a tool, the agent must choose to call it, so the discovery step stays probabilistic instead of guaranteed. Hard-coding the inventory into the system prompt is tempting. But it becomes out of date as soon as a table or page changes, and it uses context for the entire inventory on every request. Raising the turn limit only makes the waste cheaper, and the verbose discovery output still builds up in the context window. Resources are the protocol's designed answer to this problem. That is why using them is the right architectural choice over any of the workarounds.

See the MCP Resources specification, the MCP server concepts overview, and Claude Code MCP documentation for how resources are exposed and consumed.

QUESTION: A compliance review of this agent found a small share of sessions in which "process_refund" ran without a prior "get_customer" call, even though the system prompt already states that identity must be verified first. Compliance now requires that an unverified refund can never execute. Which change meets this requirement?
answers: Have the agent rate its confidence that identity was verified and skip the refund when that confidence is low.
Move the verification rule to the first line of the system prompt and add few-shot examples showing the correct call sequence.
Set "strict" to true on the "process_refund" tool definition so its inputs are grammar-constrained to the schema.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks any "process_refund" call until a verified customer ID has been returned by "get_customer".
feedbacks: A self-reported confidence score comes from the same model whose behavior is being audited. So it has the same failure modes. The model can confidently report that verification happened when it did not, and nothing outside the model checks the claim.

A more prominent position and examples can raise the compliance rate. But the model still chooses whether to follow the instruction on each turn. The requirement is that violations never run, and no prompt wording can reduce the failure rate to zero.

Strict tool use guarantees that the tool name is valid and that the input matches the JSON Schema. It says nothing about whether a business precondition, such as identity verification, has been met. A refund call can be fully valid against the schema and still be made for an unverified customer.

A PreToolUse hook runs as code before the tool call runs, and it can deny the call directly. So the refund cannot continue unless the verification precondition has really been met. This moves the rule from probabilistic model compliance to deterministic enforcement. A requirement that a call must never run needs deterministic enforcement.
prompt.explanation:
The core distinction in this scenario is between probabilistic compliance and deterministic enforcement. A system prompt rule, however prominent, is an instruction that the model weighs together with everything else in context. On most turns the model will follow it. But the audit already shows that it does not follow it every time. When a miss means an unauthorized refund, a compliance team can reasonably ask for a mechanism that cannot be skipped. That mechanism has to be in code, not in the prompt.

With client tools, Claude never runs the refund itself. It returns a tool_use block, and the application decides what to do with it. This design is what makes a code check possible. A PreToolUse hook fires before the tool runs. It inspects the pending call and can return a deny decision. The hook can check whether the session has a verified customer ID from get_customer. If it does not, the hook blocks process_refund and sends an explanation back to the model. The model then performs the verification step and retries. The guarantee comes from the fact that the check is code that runs on every call, whatever the model intended. One design point to remember: write a policy hook like this so that it denies the call whenever verification cannot be confirmed. It should not default to allow. Then the refund stays blocked even when the session state is incomplete.

The strict tool use option is the tempting wrong answer, because it also sounds like enforcement. Setting strict: true uses grammar-constrained sampling to guarantee that the tool input matches the JSON Schema and that the tool name is valid. That is a guarantee about type and shape, not about authorization. A refund request with a perfect structure for an unverified customer passes strict validation without any error. Moving the rule higher in the system prompt and adding few-shot examples makes compliance more likely, but the model still makes the decision. A self-rated confidence check asks the same model that skipped verification to confirm that it did not skip it. That adds no independent control.

QUESTION: This team added a billing-dispute subagent that the main agent delegates to after it has already called "get_customer" and "lookup_order". Logs show the subagent repeatedly replies that it has no customer record or order details to analyze. What should the team change?
answers: Add retry logic so the main agent re-invokes the subagent until it returns a complete dispute analysis.
Raise the subagent's context window allocation so the main agent's conversation history fits alongside its instructions.
State in the subagent's system prompt that it must use the customer record already retrieved by the main agent.
Include the full "get_customer" and "lookup_order" results in the prompt the main agent sends to the subagent.
feedbacks: Invoking the subagent again with the same prompt repeats the same failure. Each invocation starts fresh, without the customer and order data. Retries help with temporary faults. They do not help when an input is missing every time.
The problem is not a lack of space. The parent history is never given to a non-fork subagent, however large its context is. A larger context window does not change what content the subagent receives.

This instruction assumes the subagent can see the main agent's tool results. It cannot, because subagents do not inherit the parent's conversation history. Telling the subagent to use data that is not in its context does not make that data available.

A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context. It sees none of the main agent's conversation or tool results. The prompt string it receives is the only content that passes from the parent to the subagent. Putting the complete customer and order results in that prompt is the documented way to give the subagent what it needs.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a subagent is a separate agent instance with its own conversation. Unless it is a fork, it starts with an empty context. It receives its own system prompt from the AgentDefinition, the prompt string passed through the Agent tool, project CLAUDE.md content, and its tool definitions. It does not receive the parent's system prompt, the parent's message history, or any tool results the parent has collected. That is why the billing-dispute subagent in this scenario keeps reporting that it has nothing to analyze. The main agent called get_customer and lookup_order, but those results exist only in the main agent's context.

The isolation is deliberate. Because subagent context is kept separate, a subagent can read dozens of records or run verbose investigations, and none of that intermediate material builds up in the parent conversation. The isolation has costs, though. Each subagent spends its own tokens while it runs, and a detailed final report is still added to the parent's context when it returns. This design also means that every piece of information a subagent needs must be placed explicitly in its prompt. Anything that is not written in the delegation prompt does not exist for the subagent. For a dispute investigation, the prompt should include the complete customer record and order details. Ideally they are in a structured form that separates the data from metadata such as order IDs and timestamps.

The other approaches fail for related reasons. Telling the subagent to use a record that was "already retrieved" assumes a shared memory that the architecture does not provide. A larger context window changes capacity, not delivery, because the parent history is never sent at all. Retrying the invocation repeats the same empty handoff, because the input is missing as a result of how the system is designed, not because of a temporary problem. Note also that the exchange works the same way in the other direction. Only the subagent's final message returns to the parent. So if the main agent needs specific figures from the analysis, the subagent's prompt should ask for them explicitly.

QUESTION: Logs show the agent calls escalate_to_human on nearly every billing dispute, including ones it could resolve itself. The escalate_to_human description states clear escalation criteria, but the system prompt contains the line "CRITICAL: You MUST involve a human whenever money is disputed." answers: Add a sentiment check so the agent escalates only when the customer sounds frustrated.
Set "tool_choice" to force process_refund first so escalation can only happen after a refund attempt.
Rewrite the system prompt line into plain wording that mirrors the escalation criteria in the tool description.

feedbacks: Sentiment is an unreliable signal of whether a case really needs a human. Calm customers with real policy gaps would not be escalated. Annoyed customers with simple refunds would be escalated. This option also leaves the conflicting system prompt instruction in place, so the root cause stays.

Forcing a specific tool guarantees one particular call. But it does not stop the agent from escalating right after that call. It would also start refunds for disputes that nobody has investigated. The forced-tool option exists to guarantee the order of execution. It does not fix an instruction that is pushing tool selection in the wrong direction.

The aggressive keyword instruction in the system prompt overrides the clear limits that the tool description sets. The system prompt is part of the same tool-use context, and it strongly influences when tools are called. Replace the capitalized, absolute wording with normal wording that matches the tool description. This removes the conflict at its source, and the description then decides when the tool is selected.

The description is already clear. The problem is a conflicting instruction somewhere else. Adding more text to the description does not cancel an absolute instruction in the system prompt. When two instructions conflict, the model may follow either one. So the fix is to remove the conflict, not to try to make one side stronger.
prompt.explanation:
When a request includes tools, the API builds a tool-use system prompt. It combines the tool definitions, the developer's system prompt, and the tool configuration into one block of context. In practice, this means the system prompt and the tool descriptions are not separate layers where one takes precedence. The model reads them together. So a carefully limited description on escalate_to_human can be undone by a single line elsewhere that says CRITICAL: You MUST involve a human whenever money is disputed. Every billing dispute involves money. The keyword-based rule therefore applies to the very cases that the agent should resolve on its own, and the 80 percent first-contact resolution target cannot be reached.

Anthropic's guidance is clear on this point. Wording that was written to stop under-triggering now tends to cause over-triggering. Aggressive wording such as "CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when..." should be replaced with ordinary wording like "Use this tool when...". The most effective fix is to review the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions and rewrite them so they agree with the tool description. When the prompt and the description say the same thing in the same tone, the description's criteria can do the job they were written for. Those criteria are an explicit request for a human, policy gaps, and the agent being unable to make progress.

Each of the other approaches misses how the problem works. Expanding a description that is already clear does not cancel an absolute instruction. When two instructions contradict each other, the model may follow either one, with no reliable way to predict which. So you remove the contradiction instead of adding weight to one side. A sentiment check replaces the real escalation triggers with an unreliable signal, and it leaves the bad instruction unchanged. Forcing process_refund through tool_choice guarantees that one call happens first. That is the right tool for enforcing execution order. But it is the wrong tool for fixing a prompt that is pushing selection in the wrong direction, and it would also issue refunds before any investigation.

QUESTION: While investigating duplicate refunds in the system described above, a developer asks Claude Code to find every code path that calls "apply_refund_policy". Claude Code has already Read the file that defines the function. What should it do next?

Read every remaining file in the same directory into context so that no caller is missed.
Glob for files whose names contain "refund" and Read each of the matched files in full.
Grep for "apply_refund_policy" across file contents to find its call sites, then Read those files.
feedbacks: Guessing about code that has not been opened produces answers that are confident but not verified. That is the wrong kind of failure when the goal is to find every real caller. Anthropic's guidance is to read the relevant files before answering questions about a codebase, instead of reasoning from typical patterns.

Loading a whole directory is the anti-pattern of reading everything at the start. It uses up the context before the question is answered. It also assumes that callers are in the same place as the definition, which is often false when wrappers and services are involved.

Glob matches file names and paths, not the content inside files. So a caller in an order or billing module would be missed completely. It also loads files with "refund" in the name that never call the function, which wastes context on irrelevant content.

Finding callers is a content search. The function name appears inside the files that call it, and Grep finds that. Then Claude reads only the files that Grep returns. This follows the usage outward through wrapper modules and spends context only on files that matter.
prompt.explanation:
Building an understanding of a codebase is a repeated loop. Tracing a function's callers is the outward part of that loop. Once the definition is known, the next question is "who uses this?". The answer is written inside other files, as import statements and call expressions. That makes it a job for Grep, which searches file contents. The results give an exact list of files to Read next. Each of those files may show a wrapper or service, and Claude finds that wrapper's own callers by repeating the same search. This is how usage is traced through wrapper modules without ever loading the whole repository.

Grep answers "which files mention this identifier". Glob answers "which files have names that match this pattern". A filename search for "refund" would never find a caller of apply_refund_policy inside order_handlers.py. So Glob is the wrong tool for finding call sites, even though it is the right tool for finding, for example, every test file. The tools reference notes that Grep can return only file paths, or matching lines with line numbers. That is the kind of output a caller trace needs. On macOS, Linux, and WSL, when the standalone Grep tool is not in the default set, the same search is done with grep or rg through Bash. The strategy is the same: search contents first, then read only the files you need.

Reading every nearby file in full replaces a cheap search with a large use of context, and it still misses callers in other directories. Read is designed for targeted inspection. Its per-call limits make it unsuitable for loading many files at once. Answering from the definition alone is worse in a different way. It uses assumptions about how refund code is usually organized instead of evidence about how this code is organized. Anthropic's prompting guidance warns against this kind of guessing in agentic coding. For a duplicate-refund investigation, a list of callers that was not verified gives a false sense that every caller was found.

QUESTION: A developer on this team spent yesterday in a named Agent SDK session tracing why some refund escalations were misrouted. Overnight a teammate rewrote two of the handler files the agent had analyzed. How should the developer continue the investigation today?
answers: Resume the named session unchanged, since its saved context already reflects the handler files the agent analyzed yesterday.
Resume the session and run /compact first so the summary drops the outdated analysis of the rewritten files.
Fork the session into a new branch so the branch starts from the current contents of the rewritten files.
Resume the named session and tell the agent which two files changed so it re-reads them before continuing.
feedbacks: The saved context shows the files as they were when the agent read them, not as they are now. If the developer resumes without mentioning the rewrite, the agent reasons from file contents that no longer exist. This is the outdated tool result problem that the workflow needs to avoid.

Compaction summarizes the conversation to free context space. It has no way to know which findings are outdated, and it may keep them in the summary as if they were still true. It may also drop exact details from the parts of the investigation that are still valid.

Forking copies the conversation history into a new session ID. It does not take a snapshot of the working tree or refresh it. The forked branch inherits the same outdated analysis of the handler files. Forking solves a different problem, which is exploring alternatives from a shared starting point. It does not solve outdated information.

A session saves the conversation history, including the agent's earlier reads and conclusions about those handler files. But it does not track the filesystem. When the developer names the two rewritten files, the agent can refresh only the outdated parts of its analysis. It keeps the rest of yesterday's investigation, which costs less than exploring everything again.
prompt.explanation:
An Agent SDK session is a saved conversation: the prompts, tool calls, tool results, and responses. When a developer resumes it, the agent gets back everything it learned before. That includes the contents of files it read and the conclusions it drew from them. A session does not save the filesystem. If files changed between sessions, the agent's memory of those files is now a record of the past, not a description of the current code. Nothing in the resume mechanism reports the difference. That is why the practical rule is to tell the agent about specific file changes when resuming. The agent can then re-read only the rewritten handlers and keep the rest of yesterday's trace. It does not have to trust outdated observations or repeat the whole investigation.

Resume and fork both work on conversation history, never on the working tree. If the developer resumes the session as it is, without mentioning the changes, the analysis of code that no longer exists continues without any warning. This is how an agent ends up explaining a misrouting bug in a function that was deleted overnight. Forking creates an independent branch of the same history, so it inherits the same outdated reads. Forking exists for comparing different approaches from a shared starting point, not for refreshing state. Compaction compresses the transcript into a summary. It cannot tell findings that are still valid from findings that the rewrite made invalid. So it tends to put outdated conclusions into the summary, and it also loses exact details. Checkpointing does not help either. It tracks Claude's own edits so they can be rewound, and it does not pick up external changes made by a teammate.

When only a couple of files changed, resuming with a clear note is the right tradeoff. When most of what the agent read is outdated, a better choice is a fresh session that starts with a short structured summary of the earlier findings plus the list of changed files. Teams that often have this problem can automate the refresh with a SessionStart hook that uses the resume matcher. That hook runs on --resume and --continue. It can inject the current branch and recently modified files as additionalContext before the first prompt. See Agent SDK sessions, Claude Code hooks, and Checkpointing.

QUESTION: An engineer ran a long SDK session in which the agent investigated a billing dispute and wrote working notes to a file in the project directory. They fork that session into two branches to compare resolution strategies. The second branch's agent then reads notes that the first branch's agent wrote after the fork. What should they change?
answers: Resume the original session ID for both strategies instead of forking so all file edits stay in one transcript.
Rewind the second fork to the file checkpoint the original session captured before any notes were written.
Fork with "up_to_message_id" set to a message before any notes were written so the copy excludes them.
Run each fork in a separate working directory, since the fork copies the transcript but not files on disk.
feedbacks: Resuming the same session for both strategies gives up the goal of independent branches. It mixes both explorations into a single conversation. It also does nothing about the shared working directory, so the other run still reads the file that one run wrote.

A forked session does not carry the original session's file checkpoints. So there is no earlier checkpoint to rewind to inside the fork. File checkpointing also restores files on disk. It does not isolate branches from each other, and isolation is the real problem in this case.

The up_to_message_id parameter limits how much of the conversation transcript is copied into the fork. It has no effect on files already written to disk. The notes file would still be in the shared directory. The fork would also lose part of the investigation history that it was meant to reuse.

Forking a session copies the conversation history into a new session ID. It does not take a snapshot of the filesystem or isolate it. Both forks share the same project directory. So any file that one branch writes is real, and the other branch can see it. Giving each branch its own directory stops one branch's files from affecting the other.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, forking a session creates a branch of the conversation. The transcript up to the branch point is copied into a new session with its own ID, and the original is not changed. A session is a record of messages and tool results. It is not a snapshot of the machine. When you fork, nothing about the working directory, the environment, or the files is copied. That is why two forks from the same investigation can differ completely in what they say and how they reason, but still affect each other through anything they write to disk in a shared directory.

Anthropic's session documentation states this difference clearly. Session history is separate from file state. If a forked agent edits files in the same working directory, those edits are real, and other sessions can see them. The direct fix is to give each branch its own working directory. Then scratch files, notes, and drafts from one strategy cannot appear in the other. The design makes sense when you look at the tradeoff. Copying transcripts is cheap and safe. QUESTION: Customers often quote order numbers without the required ORD- prefix. When lookup_order receives one, it currently returns "isError" true with the text "Not found", and the agent tells the customer that no such order exists. Which tool response would let the agent recover on its own?

Return a successful result containing an empty order list so the agent asks the customer for a different number.
Return "errorCategory" set to "validation", "isRetryable" true, and a message stating the expected ORD- number format.
Return "errorCategory" set to "transient", "isRetryable" true, so the agent automatically resubmits the same lookup.
feedbacks: Retrying without any new information does not change the input. So the lookup fails the same way on every attempt, and the agent still tells the customer that the order is missing. Recovery depends on the tool result telling the agent what went wrong when the failure happens. A general retry instruction in the prompt cannot do that.

This reports a badly formatted input as a successful query with no matches. It hides the real failure and mixes up an input error with a result that is really empty. The agent would then ask the customer for another number, even though the number was correct except for the prefix. That lowers first-contact resolution.

A badly formatted order number is an input problem that the agent can fix itself, and the validation category signals this. The retryable flag and a message that states the expected format give the agent the information it needs. It can normalize the number and call lookup_order again, instead of telling the customer that the order does not exist.

A transient category tells the agent that the environment caused the failure, for example a timeout, and that the same request may succeed if repeated. In this case the input itself is wrong. So sending the same lookup again will fail every time, and the agent never learns what to change.
prompt.explanation:
The agent in this scenario can recover from a failed tool call only if the tool result tells it what kind of failure happened. MCP reports tool execution failures inside the result, with isError set to true, so the model can see the problem and correct itself. The useful detail goes in the content of that result. The protocol itself defines only the isError flag. Fields such as errorCategory and isRetryable are application-level metadata that you design into the payload. That is why their design is an architectural decision and not a protocol default.

Each error category leads to a different recovery behavior. A validation error means the input was wrong, and the agent should fix it and try again. So the error response should include a retryable flag and a message that describes the expected format. A transient error means the same request may succeed later, so retrying with backoff is appropriate. A business error means a policy refused the request, so the agent should explain instead of retrying. A permission error means the agent does not have access and should escalate. A prompt rule to retry twice uses up attempts without changing the input, because the agent still gets no feedback it can act on. Anthropic documents the same principle for client tools. It can change the outgoing arguments through updatedInput or deny the call completely. PostToolUse fires after the tool has returned, and it controls the result itself. The hook receives tool_name, tool_input, and tool_response, and it can return a replacement through updatedToolOutput. Because tool_response is untyped, normalizer code has to check each result carefully. The agent waits for ordinary hook callbacks. But if a hook reports async output, the agent continues at once. Anything the hook produces later can no longer change, block, or inject context. CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session in the project. It is meant for stable conventions and context, not for one engineer's notes on an investigation in progress. This approach fills shared project memory with one person's temporary notes. It also still loses the real conversation history and tool results.

Giving the session a display name lets you refer to it by that name. "claude --resume" with that name restores that specific conversation, whatever other sessions ran in the repository since then. This is the documented way to continue one particular earlier conversation across work sessions.

Claude Code saves each conversation as a session. A session contains the prompts, tool calls, tool results, and responses so far. The CLI gives two different ways to return to one. claude --continue (or -c) reloads the most recent conversation in the current directory. That is convenient only when nothing else has run since. claude --resume (or -r) targets a specific session by ID or by name. With no argument, it opens an interactive picker. --continue answers "what was I just doing in this directory?", and --resume answers "take me back to that particular conversation."

Names make --resume practical for work that lasts several days. A session gets a display name at launch with claude --name refund-trace, or from inside the conversation with /rename. The name then appears in /resume and in the terminal title. claude --resume refund-trace brings that conversation back with its history intact. In this scenario, other sessions run in the same repository between days. So this is the only option that reliably returns the engineer to the refund investigation, and not to whatever ran last.

The agent that confidently offered store credit would probably report high confidence, because the summary gave it no sign that anything was lost. This option also sends cases that the agent could resolve to humans, instead of fixing the information loss.

A stronger summarization prompt can reduce how often details are dropped. But summarization is still a lossy process, and each pass can still compress or leave out specific details. Instructions inside the summarizer give a probabilistic improvement, but the goal needs a structural guarantee.

Delaying summarization only moves the problem to a later point in long sessions. When the threshold is reached, the same vague condensing happens. Until then, the larger context raises cost and can make recall worse by itself.

Keep them in a structured block that is included in every prompt but never summarized. This guarantees that the agent still sees the exact commitment, however many turns have been condensed.
prompt.explanation:
The failure in this scenario is the progressive summarization trap. Each time conversation history is condensed, specific content tends to turn into abstract phrases such as "resolution preference discussed." Specific content includes amounts, percentages, dates, and especially what the customer said they would or would not accept. The summary is not wrong. It is only too vague to act on, and the agent cannot recover the original wording from a summary. Anthropic's own guidance on context engineering tools says clearly that compaction does not keep exact wording and may drop specific numbers or phrasing. That is why a summary should never be treated as the authoritative record of transactional facts.

Separate the context into two layers. The conversation history can lose detail, because most of it (greetings, clarifications, back-and-forth replies) has little value later. The small set of facts that drive decisions must not lose detail. So these facts are kept in a persistent case-facts block. The application updates this block whenever a new fact appears and inserts it again into every prompt, outside the summarized part. Code maintains the block, and the model does not regenerate it, so it stays intact through any number of summarization passes. For a support agent, this block usually holds the customer ID, order numbers, amounts, dates, issue status, and customer-stated expectations such as "refund only."

The agent then calls the tools again, so it reasons from current data instead of outdated observations.

When an Agent SDK or Claude Code session is resumed, what comes back is the saved transcript: the messages, the tool calls, and the tool results as they were recorded. Nothing runs again. When the new session starts with the summary and the agent queries the backend again, the agent keeps the continuity of the old session without its outdated data. Its best practices also note that a clean session with a good prompt often performs better than a long session with a lot of history.

Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to explain the refund limit whenever process_refund fails.

When the tool returns the violated rule this way, the agent can explain the refund limit to the customer. It can also choose a correct next step instead of guessing.

A prompt rule cannot provide information that the agent never receives. A fixed explanation in the prompt would also be wrong whenever the failure has a different cause. The agent needs the real reason in the tool result, not a guess built into its instructions.

Protocol-level JSON-RPC errors are meant for problems such as unknown tools or badly formed requests. The MCP client or host handles them. They are not given to the model as a tool result. prompt.explanation:
The Model Context Protocol deliberately separates two kinds of failure. Protocol errors are standard JSON-RPC error responses. They are reserved for problems with the call itself: an unknown tool name, arguments that fail the input schema, or an internal server fault. Tool execution errors are anything that goes wrong inside the tool's own logic, such as an upstream API failure, bad input data, or a business-rule rejection. These are returned as an ordinary JSON-RPC result whose isError field is set to true. The difference matters because the two go through different channels. The MCP client or host consumes a protocol error. A tool result is what the model receives.

In this scenario, an unhandled exception in process_refund escapes the handler and becomes a protocol error. So the agent sees only that something failed. The fix is to catch the exception and return a result with isError: true and a message that names the violated rule. This puts the failure where the agent can act on it. For a refund that is larger than the order total, the agent can then tell the customer the limit, offer a partial refund, or escalate, instead of giving a vague apology. The descriptive content next to the flag is what makes the pattern useful. The flag alone only says that something went wrong.

Each of the other approaches misses the channel problem. Adding detail to the JSON-RPC error text leaves the failure outside the tool-result path that the model reads. Returning an empty refund object as a success hides the failure completely. The agent might then tell the customer that a refund was issued. A system prompt rule cannot explain a cause that the agent was never given, and it would give the wrong explanation for failures with other causes.

Note one spelling detail. The MCP protocol field is isError in camelCase on a tools/call result. The Anthropic Messages API uses is_error in snake_case on tool_result and mcp_tool_result content blocks. They express the same idea at different layers. See the MCP tools specification, the MCP SDK error-handling guidance, and Anthropic's Handle tool calls guide.

QUESTION: The agent delegates policy research to a subagent that reads several returns-policy documents and returns a prose summary. Refund explanations then cite the wrong policy version. Which TWO changes keep each claim linked to its source document, from the subagent's input through to its report? (Select TWO.)
answers: Have the subagent attach a confidence score to each statement so the main agent can discount unsupported claims.
In the subagent's prompt, wrap each policy document in tags that keep its content and its source separate.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the subagent to remember which policy document every statement came from.
Have the subagent return each finding as a structured record pairing the claim with its source document and section.
feedbacks: Confidence scores describe how sure the subagent is, not where a claim came from. So a very confident statement can still cite the wrong policy version. Model self-ratings are also an unreliable signal. They do not bring back the source information that was lost in the summary.

Anthropic's prompting guidance recommends wrapping each document in structured tags, with separate content and source subtags. It advises against mixing the source information into the body text. When the source metadata is kept separate from the content in the input, the subagent has a clear identifier that it can return with each finding.

A prompt instruction makes correct attribution more likely, but it does not change the output format. The subagent still returns free-form text, and claims and sources get mixed together during summarization. Attribution needs a dedicated field in the returned data, not a reminder to be careful.

A subagent's intermediate reads stay inside its own context. Only its final message reaches the main agent. When the subagent returns findings as structured records that pair each claim with its source, the document name and section become part of that final message. The main agent can then name the correct policy version instead of guessing from merged free-form text.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a subagent runs in its own isolated conversation. Every document it reads and every tool result it receives stays inside that context. The parent receives only the subagent's final message. This design keeps verbose research out of the main agent's context window. But it also means that anything not in the final message is lost. When a policy subagent returns free-form text, the model naturally compresses several documents into a single narrative. The link from each statement to the document and section it came from is the first thing to disappear. The main agent then writes a fluent refund explanation that cites the wrong policy version, because it never received a reliable source for the claim.

The fix is to treat attribution as data, not as something the model should remember. In the input, wrap each policy document in structured tags with separate content and source subtags. Anthropic recommends this pattern for prompts with multiple documents. The subagent then has a clear identifier for each document, and it does not have to guess one from a heading hidden in the text. In the output, require the subagent to return findings as a structured record that pairs each claim with its source document and section. The claim-to-source mapping is kept through the handoff because it has its own field in the payload. The same structure can be passed directly into an escalation summary. A human reviewer then sees which policy clause supports a recommended refund.

The other approaches address different problems. A system prompt instruction to remember sources depends on probabilistic compliance. It leaves the output format unchanged, so claims and sources still merge in free-form text. A confidence score for each statement tells the main agent how sure the subagent is. That is unrelated to where a claim came from. A confident citation of the wrong version is still wrong, and model self-ratings are a weak signal on their own. Separating content from metadata in a structured format is the mechanism that keeps provenance (the record of where each claim came from) across agent boundaries.

See Claude prompting best practices for document structuring guidance and Subagents in the SDK for how subagent context isolation works.

QUESTION: For billing disputes that span many orders, the agent's main conversation fills with dozens of "lookup_order" results, and it later loses track of the customer's original complaint and the established case facts. Which change best keeps the main agent focused on coordination?
answers: Switch to a model with a larger context window so every order lookup fits in the conversation.
Delegate the multi-order investigation to a subagent that returns only a summary of disputed charges.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to retain the original complaint across the session.
Summarize the conversation after each "lookup_order" call so the accumulated order data stays condensed.
feedbacks: A larger window delays the problem instead of solving it. The main conversation still collects dozens of verbose tool results, and they take attention away from the complaint and the case facts. Context degradation depends on what fills the window, not only on whether the window overflows.

A default, non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context. It does not inherit the parent conversation. So the verbose order lookups build up in the subagent's context instead of in the main conversation, and only the subagent's final report comes back. The main agent keeps its context for the customer's complaint, the case facts, and the resolution decision. That is the coordination role it should keep.

An instruction to remember something does not change what is actually in the context window. When the complaint is hidden under dozens of order records, the instruction cannot bring back the information the agent needs. So the failure continues.

Repeated summarization is the mechanism that turns exact amounts, dates, and order numbers into vague, general wording. That is the same kind of loss the scenario already shows. Summarizing more often increases that risk. It does not isolate the verbose investigation.
prompt.explanation:
This is a problem of context budgeting. The main agent is doing two jobs at once: coordinating the case and running a verbose investigation. The second job is taking context away from the first. In the Claude Agent SDK, a default (non-fork) subagent is a separate agent instance that starts with a fresh context. It does not inherit the parent conversation. It receives its own system prompt plus the task prompt that the coordinator writes. When it finishes, only its final report returns to the parent. Everything it read or looked up along the way stays isolated. (Forked subagents are the documented exception. They copy the conversation so far, and that is what you do not want when the goal is to keep verbose lookups out of the main context.) This isolation is what makes delegation the right fix in this case. The dozens of lookup_order results stay only in the subagent's context. The main agent keeps the customer's complaint, the case facts, and the authority to decide on refunds or escalation.

Two practical details follow from how default subagents work. First, a default subagent starts with no knowledge of the parent conversation. So the coordinator must put the verified customer ID, the disputed amounts, and the date range directly in the delegation prompt. Anything that is not passed explicitly does not exist for the subagent. Second, the returned report still uses main-context tokens. So the subagent should be told to return a structured summary (the disputed charges, their status, and refund eligibility), not a full copy of the raw order records. The subagent can also get a restricted toolset, for example only lookup_order, so it cannot process refunds on its own.

The other approaches fail for related reasons. A larger context window changes the point where overflow happens. It does not change the fact that verbose tool output pushes aside the facts the agent needs. A system prompt reminder cannot bring back information that is hidden or was lost through compression. Instructions affect behavior, not what the window contains. Summarizing after every lookup makes the problem worse. Progressive summarization is what turns exact figures and order numbers into vague phrases, and the scenario already shows the agent losing track of case facts. A dedicated non-fork subagent isolates the investigation at its source. This pattern protects the coordinator's context without losing precision.

See Subagents in the Agent SDK and Claude Code subagents for how subagent context isolation, forks, and reporting work.

QUESTION: The agent's drafted billing-dispute replies sometimes leave out the refund timeline or the policy clause that was applied. Each reply is written in one step, so the team cannot see where details get lost. What design change best addresses both problems?
answers: Split the reply into separate draft, checklist-review, and refine calls, and log each stage's output.
Add few-shot examples of complete billing-dispute replies showing the timeline and policy clause.
Automatically regenerate any reply shorter than the median resolution length until it passes a size check.
Restate the required reply elements in capitals at the top of the system prompt and in every turn.
feedbacks: This is the self-correction form of prompt chaining. A draft call writes the reply. A review call checks the draft against explicit completeness criteria. A refine call applies the review. Each stage is a separate call, so the application can log and inspect the intermediate outputs. The logs show where the timeline or policy clause is lost, and the review stage catches the missing detail before the customer sees the reply.

Few-shot examples are a valid way to make it more likely that a reply includes the required elements. But they work inside the same single generation step. They do not show where details are lost. Compliance also stays probabilistic, because nothing checks the reply. So this option only partly addresses one of the two problems.

Reply length does not show whether the refund timeline or policy clause is present. A retry based on size can accept incomplete replies and reject complete short ones. Retrying the same single step also adds cost and latency, and it does not show where the detail is lost.

Stronger wording and repetition only change how much weight these instructions have compared with other instructions. They still depend on the model noticing them during one pass. The reply is still a single step that cannot be inspected. So the team cannot see where the failure happens, and nothing checks that the elements are present.
prompt.explanation:
Sometimes a single generation step produces output that is usually right but sometimes incomplete. The architectural fix is to stop treating the reply as one step that cannot be inspected, and instead to chain it into explicit stages. Anthropic calls this explicit prompt chaining: breaking a task into sequential calls. It is still valuable when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure. The documented self-correction pattern fits this scenario directly. Generate a draft. Have Claude review that draft against concrete criteria (refund timeline present, policy clause cited, next steps stated). Then have Claude refine the draft based on the review. Each stage is its own call, so the application can log, evaluate, or branch between any two stages.

A chain costs a little more latency and tokens. In return, it gives two things that a single step cannot give: an observable failure point and a structural check. Suppose the draft contains the timeline but the final reply does not. The logs then show that the refine stage dropped it. If the draft never had the timeline, the review stage reports the gap and the refine stage fixes it. The same reasoning explains why a large code review is split into one pass per file followed by an integration pass. Focused stages produce consistent depth. The handoff between stages also becomes a place where you can measure quality instead of assuming it. In the Agent SDK, the agent loop itself handles tool calls and results. A staged reply pipeline is an application-level structure built on top of that loop. The SDK's per-message objects make it easy to record what each stage produced.

The other approaches all stay inside the single step. Few-shot examples and strong prompt wording make it more likely that the model includes the required elements, and that is useful. But they are probabilistic guidance. Nothing checks the result, and nothing shows where a miss starts. A length-based retry replaces the real requirement with an indirect measure (reply size). So it can accept incomplete replies and reject good short ones. It also spends extra tokens on regeneration that teaches the team nothing. Only the chained design turns an omission that happens sometimes and cannot be seen into a sequence that is logged, can be reviewed, and can be corrected.

See Claude prompting best practices for guidance on chaining complex prompts and sequential steps, and the Agent SDK agent loop for how messages and results are returned in the SDK.
